#10359. NowThis just bought one of Gen Z’s favorite Instagram news accounts. Here’s why

If Instagram is your preferred avenue for media consumption, you’ve probably come across posts by Impact. The popular Gen-Z-targeted account is characterized by its quick-turn analysis on progressive, left-wing topics ranging from identity politics to mental health and niche internet trends. That winning formula caught the attention of social video publisher NowThis, which recently acquired the brand.

Launched in 2020 by founders Tim Chau and Michelle Andrews, the Impact Instagram handle was born in the apex of Gen Z’s formative years, an era marked by a hyper-online generation who reckoned with Donald Trump, COVID-19, social isolation, canceled graduations, the murder of George Floyd, and climate disaster all in the same year. Impact created timely stories around narratives that Gen Z desperately craved and traditional media often failed to cover: Its content is often among the first to share pointed commentary on trending headlines. 

When comedian Shane Gillis was being criticized online for a misogynistic SNL bit, Impact published “Male comedians don’t actually have to hate women to be popular.” After the internet was in an uproar over the U.K. banning books authored by Sally Rooney due to her support for Palestine, Impact wrote about it immediately. Impact even creates content around shared woes that span multiple generations, helping it reach larger audiences—as seen in posts like “Is it rude to ask friends to stay with them when you visit their city?” The comments section of each post is the heart of the community the Impact team has built and a glimpse into real cultural capital, making it easy to see why NowThis chose to purchase the company. 

Founded in 2012 by former Huffington Post execs Kenneth Lerer and Eric Hippeau, NowThis began as a social-first go-to for millennial content before being acquired by Vox Media. As millennials aged into the next phase of adulthood, companies and news organizations from all corners of the internet competed for the coveted attention of young people, nudging the video publisher into a new chapter. In 2023, NowThis expanded into a large-scale media network targeting Gen Z, taking on a new CEO, Sharon Mussalli, and a new editor-in-chief, Michael Vito Valentino, while also reckoning with the ramifications of significant layoffs. This latest move in acquiring Impact—for an alleged seven-figure all-cash deal—demonstrates a commitment to reaching its target audience and the community of young people behind Impact. 

“[They] care about what’s happening in the world and want to understand how it connects to their relationships, their work, their culture, and their futures. That’s closely aligned with the Gen Z female audience we’re building for at NowThis. And we saw an opportunity to invest in that relationship and give it more room to grow,” Mussalli said in a statement via the NowThis PR team. 

She adds: “Impact brings a distinct editorial voice and a strong sense of what resonates with its community. We bring the production capabilities and experience developing original video franchises to help translate that into new series and recurring formats. Our ambition is to build something this audience can grow with, across all NowThis channels. That means giving people more than an individual story they encounter in their feed—it means creating recognizable programming they seek out, share, and return to.” 

In a statement to Fast Company, Chau, who is stepping down from the Impact staff but will remain involved in some capacity, calls the move “bittersweet.” “We put everything into Impact to get it where it is today, so stepping back isn’t easy. But we couldn’t be happier about where it’s headed, because we know NowThis is the right home for it. They’re leading in a space where social now dominates—really the first of their kind—and that’s exactly the future we want Impact to be part of.”

“My hope is that Impact stays the place young people go to for stories that actually land with them, the ones they talk about with friends, share, and sit with. Legacy media has struggled to resonate with this generation, and I hope Impact can keep being the place where they feel truly understood and connected,” Chau said.

#10358. Easily Build and Share ROCm Kernels with Hugging Face

Custom kernels are the backbone of high-performance deep learning, enabling GPU operations tailored precisely to your workload; whether that’s image processing, tensor transformations, or other compute-heavy tasks. But compiling these kernels for the right architectures, wiring all the build flags, and integrating them cleanly into PyTorch extensions can quickly become a mess of CMake/Nix, compiler errors, and ABI issues, which is not fun. Hugging Face’s kernels library makes it easy to build (with kernel-builder) and share these kernels with the kernels-community, with support for multiple GPU and accelerator backends, including CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and XPU. This ensures your kernels are fast, portable, and seamlessly integrated with PyTorch.

In this guide, we focus exclusively on ROCm-compatible kernels and show how to build, test, and share them using kernels. You’ll learn how to create kernels that run efficiently on AMD GPUs, along with best practices for reproducibility, packaging, and deployment.

This ROCm-specific walkthrough is a streamlined version of the original kernel-builder guide. If you’re looking for the broader CUDA-focused version, you can find it here: A Guide to Building and Scaling Production-Ready CUDA Kernels.

We will use the GEMM kernel from RadeonFlow_Kernels as an example. If you want to go straight to the guide, click here.

This section was written by the RadeonFlow GEMM kernel authors to introduce the kernel.Authors: ColorsWind, Zesen Liu, and Andy

The RadeonFlow GEMM kernel is a high-performance, FP8 block-wise matrix multiplication implementation optimized for the AMD Instinct MI300X GPU. GEMM (General Matrix Multiplication) is the core building block behind most deep learning workloads: given two matrices A and B, you compute their product C = A × B. Here it’s implemented in FP8, a low-precision floating-point format that trades a bit of accuracy for much higher throughput and lower memory bandwidth. This kernel was developed for the AMD Developer Challenge 2025, it was awarded the 🏆 Grand Prize in June 2025, recognizing its excellence in performance and innovation on AMD hardware.

The kernel operates on quantized inputs using the e4m3fnuz floating-point format and applies per-block scaling to preserve accuracy during low-precision computation. The e4m3fnuz format is an FP8 variant with 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits, designed to be efficient for neural network workloads. Because FP8 has a much smaller dynamic range than FP16/FP32, we apply per-block scaling factors (a_scale and b_scale) so that each block of values is rescaled into a numerically “comfortable” range before and after computation, which helps preserve accuracy despite the low precision. It takes the following arguments:

where a and b are the input matrices, a_scale and b_scale are the scaling factors for a and b respectively, and c is the output matrix:

The kernel is precompiled for specific matrix shapes and assumes a transposed memory layout (as required by the competition). To support additional shapes or alternative memory layouts, you must modify the kernel launcher.

So now that we have a high-performance ROCm kernel, the natural question is: how do we integrate it into a real PyTorch workflow and share it with others? That’s exactly what we’ll cover next, using kernels to structure, build, and publish the ROCm kernel.

This is a fairly technical guide, but you can still follow it step by step without understanding every detail and everything will work fine. If you’re curious, you can always come back later to dig deeper into the concepts.

This file orchestrates the entire build. It tells the kernel-builder what to compile and how everything connects.

#10357. A new report says free childcare in NYC will pay for itself

Since taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made it his mission to expand access to affordable childcare in the city, and for good reason. On average, NYC families spend $21,000 on childcare annually per child—equaling an estimated $10 billion citywide every year. While about 40% of children in the city receive some free or subsidized care, the remaining 60% receive none, leaving many families to pay entirely out of pocket.

A new report reveals how universal childcare would not only benefit families in New York City, but also boost the economy: Just 35 hours of free childcare per week could bring up to $6.5 billion in economic value each year, which would likely exceed the cost of providing that care. 

The report—which was produced by a nonpartisan think tank, the 5BORO Institute at Citizens Union, in partnership with Boston Consulting Group—surveyed more than 2,700 parents of children younger than 5, along with about a hundred families who moved away from New York City recently. 

According to the report, nearly 70% of children under the age of 6 are cared for by parents or adults who work. When those parents are unable to find care and forced to drop out of the workforce or switch jobs, the city loses $1.7 billion in annual income; among the parents surveyed, 15% altered their work situation due to childcare issues. For hourly workers, childcare gaps can force them to miss out on $360 million in earnings each year. The report also found that childcare was a leading concern for families who had left the city, a growing trend that is supported by plenty of other data. 

In other words, employers also feel the effects of inadequate access to care. That can mean high turnover or simply lost productivity if their workers regularly contend with disruptions to their childcare: More than half of the parents surveyed said they had missed at least one full day of work over the past three months, averaging three to four missed days.

These childcare gaps can cost New York City employers about 54 million hours of missed work, according to the report. The act of providing 35 hours of free childcare each week would also enable nearly 30,000 parents to reenter the workforce, which could yield more than a billion dollars in annual earnings.

Childcare has been a key focus for Mamdani since his campaign, and as Fast Company reported in a recent cover story, the mayor has even gotten the business community on board with its investments in this area. Mamdani is already building upon the universal 3-K program established by former Mayor Bill de Blasio to extend care to younger children; the recently launched 2-K program is now providing free, full-day childcare to 2,000 2-year-olds, with plans to serve an additional 10,000 children by next fall. (The city has provided free pre-K to all 4-year-olds since 2014.) 

Even business leaders who are critical of Mamdani have seemingly come around to the idea of free childcare, though they may not agree on how to achieve that. This fall, the 5BORO Institute created the NYC Child Care Business Council, bringing together a number of business leaders and organizations committed to putting their muscle behind this issue and advocating for childcare investment (something the business community has not historically done).

For years, employers have invested in generous parental leave policies and backup childcare benefits for their workforce to help them court top talent and retain some of their best employees. But it seems companies are finally realizing that their best efforts can’t make up for a lack of robust childcare options or offset the mounting cost of care.

“The market is not able to solve this problem,” Grace Rauh, the executive director of Citizens Union, recently told Fast Company. Citizens Union is a nonpartisan nonprofit founded in 1897 to promote government accountability, ethics, transparency, and civic engagement across New York. “Frankly, private businesses aren’t able to provide the kind of fully robust childcare benefits that their employees need,” Rauh said.

#10356. Why Transactional Emails Fail After Deployment: A Practical Debugging Guide for Developers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Transactional emails are easy to overlook during application development. A registration form works, the database stores the user's information, and the backend successfully triggers an email. Everything appears to be functioning as expected.

Then a user reports that their password-reset message never arrived.

The problem might not be in the email template or the sending function. It could involve DNS configuration, authentication failures, message formatting, queue processing, recipient-server policies, or an incorrectly configured production environment.

For developers building SaaS applications, ecommerce platforms, and web services, reliable email delivery is an important part of the user experience. An account-verification message that never arrives can prevent someone from accessing an application, while a delayed security notification can create unnecessary confusion.

Understanding how to investigate these problems requires looking beyond the email-sending function. This guide explores a practical debugging workflow, the technical layers involved, and the tools developers can use to identify common email delivery failures.

One of the first mistakes developers make when troubleshooting email is assuming that a successful API response means the message has reached the recipient.

When an application submits an email through an SMTP server or an email service provider's API, the provider may accept the request and return a successful response. However, the receiving mail server still needs to process the message.

Depending on its configuration and policies, the receiving server might:

Accept the message and place it in the inbox.

Accept the message but classify it as spam.

Reject the message because of authentication or policy issues.

Accept the message but place it in another folder.

A successful request therefore confirms only that a particular stage of the process completed.

Developers should distinguish between three important states:

Submission: The application successfully handed the message to its sending provider.

Acceptance: The receiving mail server accepted responsibility for the message.

Inbox placement: The message became visible in the recipient's expected inbox.

These distinctions make troubleshooting considerably easier. Instead of immediately rewriting an email template, developers can identify which stage is actually failing.

Before investigating external email infrastructure, examine the application's own implementation.

A common example is a password-reset workflow. The application receives a request, generates a temporary token, creates a reset URL, and sends an email containing that URL.

Several problems can occur before the message even reaches an email provider.

The application generates an expired token.

The reset URL points to a staging environment.

An asynchronous task fails before processing the message.

The email service credentials are incorrect.

An API request times out without being retried.

The application records success before confirming the provider's response.

Start by logging the important stages of the process.

For example, a Node.js application might use structured logging:

This example assumes that the email provider returns a message identifier. Adapt the response fields to the actual SDK being used.

Notice that the logs identify the recipient through an internal ID rather than exposing their complete email address.

Avoid logging passwords, authentication tokens, reset URLs, or other sensitive information.

The objective is to establish a traceable record of what happened without introducing additional security risks.

Email authentication is another important area to investigate when messages are rejected or consistently classified as spam.

Three commonly used mechanisms help receiving servers evaluate whether a message is authorized to represent a particular domain.

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allows a domain owner to specify which servers are authorized to send messages using that domain.

This information is published through DNS.

A simplified SPF record might look like this:

The actual record must reflect the sending services authorized by the domain owner.

Forgetting to authorize a new email provider.

Publishing multiple SPF records for the same domain.

Leaving outdated sending services in the record.

Remember that SPF evaluates the sending infrastructure against the envelope sender domain. It does not automatically guarantee that the visible From address is aligned.

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages.

The receiving server can retrieve the corresponding public key through DNS and verify that the signature is valid.

A mismatch between the configured selector and published record.

Developers integrating multiple email providers should verify that each provider has the correct signing configuration.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) builds on SPF and DKIM.

It allows domain owners to define how receiving servers should handle messages that fail authentication and alignment requirements.

A basic monitoring-oriented DMARC record might look like this:

This is an illustrative configuration. The reporting address must be valid, and the domain should have an appropriate monitoring and policy-enforcement plan.

Developers can use MXToolbox to inspect DNS records and investigate common authentication problems.

For additional technical background, SitePoint's guide to HTML email development explains why email environments require different implementation considerations from ordinary web pages.

An email template that looks perfect in a browser can behave differently when rendered by Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail, or another email client.

This happens because email clients do not implement HTML and CSS in exactly the same way.

A layout may break because of unsupported CSS properties, image restrictions, unexpected font rendering, or differences in how tables are handled.

For this reason, email testing should be part of the development process rather than something performed only after users report a problem.

HTML validation: Check the markup for malformed elements, missing attributes, and unnecessary code.

Rendering tests: Preview the email across desktop and mobile email clients.

Link verification: Confirm that buttons, links, and personalized URLs point to the correct destinations.

Image testing: Check whether the message remains understandable when images are blocked.

Content inspection: Review subject lines, sender information, and the plain-text alternative.

Deliverability checks: Examine authentication, content-related warnings, and potential inbox placement problems.

Developers can also incorporate pre-send diagnostics into their release workflow to identify potential deliverability problems before a message is sent to a larger audience.

The important point is to treat these checks as one part of quality assurance, not as a guarantee that every message will reach the primary inbox.

For more information about email rendering differences, SitePoint's article on essential HTML email coding tips provides useful examples of client-specific behavior.

Testing transactional emails with real customer addresses during development can create unnecessary problems.

A better approach is to use a dedicated testing environment that captures outgoing messages without delivering them to actual recipients.

For example, Mailpit provides a local SMTP server and web interface for inspecting messages during development.

The final output generated by the application.

Another option is Mailtrap, which provides email testing capabilities for development workflows.

Consider a registration feature that sends a welcome message whenever a new user creates an account.

Instead of sending hundreds of test messages to real addresses, developers can configure the development environment to capture them in a testing inbox.

This makes it possible to repeatedly test different templates without affecting actual customers or generating unnecessary email traffic.

A separate testing environment also reduces the risk of accidentally sending development notifications to production users.

Applications that send large numbers of emails often use background workers instead of processing every message during the original HTTP request.

This approach helps keep the application responsive, but it introduces another potential source of failures.

Imagine an ecommerce application that sends order confirmations after checkout.

The application creates an order successfully and places an email task in a queue. However, the background worker becomes unavailable before processing the task.

The customer receives an order confirmation much later than expected, or perhaps not at all.

To investigate these problems, developers should monitor:

Retries are particularly important, but they need to be implemented carefully.

A temporary network failure may justify another attempt. A permanent rejection caused by an invalid recipient address usually does not.

Exponential backoff can help prevent repeated requests from overwhelming an unavailable service.

In a production system, add random jitter to avoid having multiple workers retry simultaneously.

Also consider idempotency. If a worker processes the same task twice, the application should avoid sending duplicate transactional messages whenever possible.

A reliable queue architecture should distinguish between temporary failures and permanent failures rather than retrying every error indefinitely.

Testing before deployment is important, but it cannot reveal every issue that may occur in production.

Real email traffic introduces changing conditions, including recipient-server behavior, sender reputation, invalid addresses, and differences between email providers.

Developers should therefore establish ongoing monitoring.

For Gmail-related monitoring, Google Postmaster Tools provides information about domain reputation, spam rates, and authentication.

It is particularly useful for teams sending enough email to generate meaningful reporting data.

Another useful resource is Can I Email, which documents HTML and CSS feature support across email clients.

These tools address different problems. Monitoring sender reputation will not fix a broken password-reset URL, just as validating HTML will not resolve a DNS authentication failure.

The best approach is to monitor each layer independently.

A repeatable checklist helps developers investigate problems without overlooking important details.

Before releasing a new email feature, review the following:

Confirm that the application successfully submits the message.

Verify that provider credentials and environment variables are correct.

Inspect SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration.

Validate the HTML and plain-text versions.

Preview the message on desktop and mobile email clients.

Verify that development and production configurations are separated.

Check delivery events and provider error reports.

Monitor bounce and complaint rates after deployment.

Not every application needs an expensive testing platform or a complicated monitoring stack.

A small project might only require a local email testing environment, basic DNS checks, and structured application logs.

A larger SaaS platform may benefit from automated integration tests, provider webhooks, queue monitoring, authentication reports, and dedicated deliverability testing.

The right setup depends on the application's sending volume, complexity, and the importance of its email workflows.

Reliable email delivery requires more than calling an SMTP function or integrating an email API.

Developers need to understand the complete process, from application logic and message construction to authentication, queue processing, recipient-server acceptance, and inbox placement.

The most effective troubleshooting strategy is to isolate these layers instead of treating every missing message as a template problem.

Start with application logs, inspect provider responses, validate authentication records, test email rendering, and monitor production behavior.

By incorporating these checks into development and deployment workflows, teams can reduce avoidable failures and build applications that communicate more reliably with their users.

#10355. Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors

Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

#10354. Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang had one message: It’s business as usual

Nvidia on Tuesday held its first earnings call in its 33-year history without cofounder Jensen Huang, who resigned five days ago after a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy. After reporting strong third-quarter numbers, interim CEO Colette Kress (who has been Nvidia’s CFO since 2013) kept the call focused on Nvidia’s immediate business concerns. 

Analysts wanted to know what the company would say about the succession plan after Huang’s departure, and about the future of Nvidia’s pivotal role as the company powering the AI race. 

Most of the salient information about Huang was given at the front of the call by Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair of the board. Jones said Nvidia doesn’t intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO, providing a clapback to the growing contingent on social media lobbying for the ousted CEO’s return. Jones said the executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles is handling the search for a new CEO, but that Nvidia is looking at both internal and external candidates for the job. 

“The board is acting deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees and investors,” Jones said. “With that we will take no further questions about the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation.”

The numbers

Kress then took over the call and kept things focused on Nvidia’s numbers. Kress has run Nvidia’s earnings calls for years, but always alongside Huang, who set the company’s vision and did much of its dealmaking with customers and partners. Today her main job was to report the quarterly numbers, and convince investors that the world’s most important AI chip company can run without its founder.

The numbers, at least, are good. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for its fiscal third quarter, well above Wall Street’s roughly $109 billion forecast, and projected $130 billion for the current quarter. Investors expected a beat. 

Kress said Nvidia has seen “explosive” adoption of its latest Vera Rubin computing platform, which includes a Rubin GPU and a Vera CPU. “Our momentum is real,” she said. “Our ambition will not change, our passion for innovation will not change.” 

Revenue for the quarter came in at $115.8 billion, about $6.5 billion higher than the roughly $109 billion analysts expected. Adjusted earnings were $2.68 per share, 21 cents above the $2.47 consensus. 

But all that happened during a third quarter that ended October 25—that is, before the Huang scandal broke. That’s why analysts were more concerned about the guidance numbers for a future without Huang. Some analysts had even questioned whether Nvidia would venture to give a full year 2028 guidance. 

But it did. For the short term, Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion. The company had previously said it expects to see 70% growth in 2028, but Kress said its moving that guidance up to 75% growth, citing continued strong demand for AI infrastructure, including Vera Rubin, and despite the chance that chip exports to China will constrict somewhat in the wake of the Huang scandal.

That may have settled some analysts’ nerves about the AI sell-off that started in October, which was driven by the fear that Big Tech companies would slow their spending on AI data centers. 

Why this call mattered

Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, resigned on November 12 amid two scandals. The first involved an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence believe may have been spying for China. Beijing has strongly denied the allegations. Nvidia’s board has opened an internal investigation into whether company or national security secrets were compromised. Huang stepped down shortly after reports of a second alleged affair, this one with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare (and the CEO’s direct report).

The board made Kress interim CEO. She also stays on as CFO until a permanent CEO is named. Longtime director Harvey Jones became Nvidia’s first board chair. 

The stock was already falling before the scandal. Nvidia closed at a record $239.24 on October 6. Shares then fell on fears that AI spending would slow, and fell further as the Huang story unfolded. By Tuesday the stock was below $154, its lowest level since mid-2025. That’s a loss of about $2 trillion in market value. That’s why Wall Street was listening to Kress so closely. 

Before the call, analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives predicted Kress would talk very little about Huang, that her main job would be to “restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward,” he told Fox Business. 

And that’s exactly what happened. After the brief section at the front, the call had a business-as-usual tone, complete with a blizzard of numbers showing that Nvidia—as of the third quarter, at least—continues to sit at the center of the AI world.

#10353. Apriel-H1: The Surprising Key to Distilling Efficient Reasoning Models

We converted our 15B reasoning model to a Mamba hybrid achieving 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss. The key? A non-obvious insight about what data to distill on, and why intuition fails here.

When MiniMax published their M2 post-mortem in October explaining why they abandoned efficient attention at 230B scale, the narrative briefly became "efficient attention is dead." Within days, Kimi Linear proved otherwise. The real lesson: it depends on your constraints.

Our constraint was simple: we had a strong 15B reasoning model and needed to make it efficient without starting over. No infinite compute for 20T-token pretraining. No luxury of architectural co-design from day one. Just a practical question: can you retrofit efficiency into an existing model through distillation?

Spoilers: yes, but only if you ignore your intuition about what data to use.

The Apriel-H1 family: seven checkpoints spanning 25-40 Mamba layers (out of 50 total), showing the complete efficiency-quality frontier. Our flagship Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT achieves 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss: MATH500 and MTBench improve a few points (0.90 → 0.92 and 8.30 → 8.58, respectively), while GSM8k (0.97 → 0.95), GPQA (0.59 → 0.55), and AIME24 (0.70 → 0.65) regress slightly. Total training: 76.8B tokens.

Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT (green) vs full-attention teacher (blue). Reasoning quality stays nearly flat across benchmarks while throughput increases 1.89-2.09x depending on context length.

The full details are in our Apriel-H1 paper. Here, we focus on the key insight that made it work.

Here's what we initially thought would work: just distill on pretraining data and round it out with some SFT.

The reasoning seemed solid. We're inserting completely new Mamba layers that have never seen data. These linear SSMs need to learn general-purpose token mixing from scratch. How can they become effective mixers unless they get exposure to the same broad distribution the original attention layers saw?

So we tried it. Then we tried mixing pretraining and SFT data. It didn't work. The distilled hybrids lost reasoning quality, sometimes dramatically.

What actually worked: high-quality reasoning traces from the teacher's SFT dataset.

Distilling a reasoning model isn't about transferring general next-token prediction. The base model already has that, and we started from a strong 15B foundation. What we're preserving is specific and fragile: the teacher's multi-step reasoning patterns.

Those patterns emerge from intricate attention mechanisms. Retrieval heads pulling context from thousands of tokens back. Induction heads recognizing and continuing logical chains. Long-range dependencies connecting premises to conclusions many steps later. When you replace attention wholesale with Mamba's linear recurrence, these computational mechanisms are disrupted. The hybrid must discover new paths to the same reasoning outcomes.

That discovery requires explicit examples where reasoning structure is visible and correct:

Pretraining data, on the other hand, is too noisy and too diffuse. The reasoning signal gets lost. You need concentrated examples of the specific capability you're trying to preserve.

Once we understood the data choice, our distillation method became clear too. We used reverse KL divergence (temperature 1) rather than forward KL. Reverse won consistently. Why? We're training on problems where the teacher has high confidence and clear structure. Reverse KL's mode-seeking behavior encourages the student to commit to those high-confidence predictions. When your teacher is confident and correct, you want your student to be confident too.

This insight is the key to the whole approach: match your distillation data to the capability you're preserving, not the capability you're building.

You can't just swap 40 attention layers for Mamba and hope. We learned this the hard way, and eventually developed a staged distillation procedure to get there reliably.

Stage 1: Identify least-important layers. We used a Leave-One-Out (LOO) analysis on MMLU: remove each layer, replace with identity, then measure the drop. Sort by importance, replace the bottom 25 with Mamba-in-Llama (MIL) initialized mixers. Distill end-to-end. This worked for our H-25 checkpoint.

Stage 2: Progressive conversion beyond 25 layers. LOO broke down past 25 layers because layers unimportant in isolation became critical in combination. To address this, we developed a dynamic heuristic we call MIL-Mamba-Replacement (MMR). For each remaining attention layer, we initialize a Mamba mixer with MIL, run 100 training steps, and record the distillation loss. Layers converging to lower loss are "easier" to replace. This captures training dynamics rather than static importance.

We progressed incrementally: 25 → 27 → 30 → 34 → 37 → 40 Mamba layers, grouping replacements by MMR scores. Each checkpoint distills from the previous.

Stage 3: End-to-end training on SFT data. After reaching the target Mamba layer count, we did a final SFT pass until reasoning performance stabilized. After 55.9B distillation tokens and 20.9B SFT tokens, this produced our final Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT model.

The complete efficiency frontier. Each checkpoint shows cumulative training tokens. Our flagship H-30-SFT (released as Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT) used 76.8B total for 2.1x throughput at 0.76 average score. The aggressively converted H-40 variant used 136.5B tokens for 3.4x throughput. For reference: NVIDIA's Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 achieves 4.6x at 0.77 score but required training from scratch with orders of magnitude more compute.

We built all this on Fast-LLM, our open-source training framework. The core architectural principle: large language model transformers should be modular. Attention and Mamba are different implementations of the same "mixing" interface, and can be swapped freely.

Here's a hybrid architecture in Fast-LLM's config format:

The pattern field specifies layer order. For Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT: 30 mamba_block, 20 attention_block, placed by importance. That's it.

Fast-LLM handles gradient accumulation, distributed training, tensor parallelism, checkpointing, everything you need for large-scale experimentation. It's open source, and licensed under Apache 2.0. You can reproduce this work because we designed the infrastructure to make it reproducible.

Why release all checkpoints? Because optimal depends on your constraints. H-30 offers the best balance. H-40 maximizes throughput for latency-critical workloads. The intermediate checkpoints let you choose your exact trade-off.

Why do you get different speedups at different context lengths? Mamba's linear complexity advantage grows with sequence length, and attention degrades quadratically.

Why did you only try Mamba? We used Mamba-1 for three reasons: it has a proven distillation track record, has shown strong empirical performance, and was simple to implement in our framework. It let us focus on the data question first.

What were the Mamba hyperparameters? State size 16, DT rank 16, inner dimension 4096. For our GQA setup in Apriel we expanded B (input projection) and x (state) to match total attention heads following M1.

Why didn't you try more advanced conversion methods? We used Mamba-in-Llama initialization and knowledge distillation rather than MOHAWK's multi-stage procedure because the latter didn't show significant advantages in preliminary experiments.

Why did you only SFT the H-30 model? We only applied SFT to H-30 to validate that distilled hybrids can be improved through standard post-training. The other checkpoints are pure distillation but can be fine-tuned similarly.

Why didn't you explore RL? This was a scoping decision to isolate the distillation question: can you transfer reasoning via knowledge distillation alone? Answer: yes. But RL should close remaining quality gaps further. We are exploring RL for future iterations.

Did you really show that Apriel-H1 matches full-attention reasoning at similar compute budgets? We didn't do an apples-to-apples comparison between full-attention Apriel and a hybrid trained identically from pretraining forward. That would require repeating all mid-training and post-training of the teacher with the Apriel-H1 architecture, which was beyond our compute budget. What we can claim though is that retrofitting efficiency via distillation is practical and effective, and that the resulting hybrids can be fine-tuned to match or exceed the teacher's reasoning quality.

We've implemented Apriel-H1 in Hugging Face Transformers and vLLM. Transformers integration is straightforward. We ship a new model class with interchangeable attention and Mamba layers. vLLM integration uses their recent Mamba cache operations for continuous batching, prefix caching, and chunked prefill. The vLLM plugin is ready. We are currently waiting for final legal approval to open-source it.

Honest assessment: Deploying hybrids today means rough edges. The tooling is maturing fast but isn't turnkey. You will write custom code, validate numerical behavior carefully, and work around framework limitations. For teams that can absorb that cost, throughput gains are worth it. For those that can't, waiting might be the right call.

Most teams don't have infinite compute for 20T-token pretraining. If you've invested in a strong base model and need efficiency gains, this work shows a practical path: distill into hybrids using high-quality task-specific data that matches the capability you're preserving.

The surprising finding, use reasoning data to distill reasoning, seems obvious in retrospect but contradicts initial intuition. We validated it, explained why it works, and built the infrastructure to make it reproducible.

Models: Apriel-H1 Collection on HuggingFaceTraining framework: Fast-LLM on GitHubTeacher model: Apriel-Nemotron-15B-ThinkerPaper: Apriel-H1: Towards Efficient Enterprise Reasoning Models

Found something broken? File an issue. Discovered a better layer placement heuristic? Tell us. Built something interesting on Apriel-H1? We'd love to see it.

#10352. Why the smartest AI strategy starts with a little laziness

My employees know that I have an unconventional take on laziness: A lazy mindset doesn’t mean being unproductive. Often, it means finding a faster way to get something done. As Bill Gates famously said, “I choose a lazy person to do a hard job. Because a lazy person will find an easy way to do it.”

That’s why I encourage a lazy mindset, insofar as it means looking for more efficient ways to get things done—like leveraging the latest AI and automation tools. As I’ve seen in leading a company of more than 800 employees, people are eager to streamline their work. Studies confirm they’re doing it, whether their employers know about it or not.

One recent report found that while only 40% of companies surveyed had purchased official subscriptions to large language models, employees at more than 90% of those companies reported regular use of artificial intelligence. That often leads to piecemeal adoption and missed opportunities to realize AI’s full potential. Studies suggest AI can absorb 60% to 70% of busywork, freeing employees to focus on more meaningful tasks, like strategizing and coming up with innovative solutions.

Leaders should recognize this reality and adopt AI initiatives at the enterprise level. But the challenge isn’t finding opportunities—there are countless AI tools on the market, and more rolling out every day. It’s deciding which are worth pursuing. Every AI initiative comes with trade-offs, requiring time, budget, talent, and executive approval. Here are some tips for taking a more strategic approach to AI adoption in your company.

Start with business goals, not AI tools

Estimates of the number of AI tools on the market vary widely, from around 2,500 to more than 50,000. (If you look at live, available products, the lower figure is likely more accurate.) But one thing is indisputable: There are a ton, more than anyone could possibly test while working a full-time job. Amid this dizzying array of options, the first step in integrating AI into an organization is top down, clarifying your broader business goals.

Maybe your primary objective is to make it easier for users to incorporate your software into their everyday lives. AI-powered chatbots that field recurring user questions could be a wise investment. Or maybe your goal is to analyze users’ circumstances quickly and provide help faster. A tool that uses AI to analyze and synthesize vast amounts of data could transform your business. In healthcare, for example, IBM’s Watson has been used to analyze patient data and medical literature and provide doctors with evidence-based treatment options.

The key is to start with the problem you want to solve, not the technology you’re excited to use.

When leaders define their business goals, they can focus on AI opportunities that align with those goals and avoid the myriad distractions out there. Rather than dedicating resources to tools that merely speed things up, they can focus on uses with the greatest potential impact. They can deliberately pass on AI tools that don’t align with business objectives and concentrate their efforts where AI can make the biggest difference.

Let employees lead the way

If you were developing new cooking technology for a bakery, you probably wouldn’t begin with the product designer. You’d start by asking the baker how they work, where things tend to go awry, and how you might improve their processes. The best ideas for improving how people work often come from those on the front lines.

At my company, we invite all employees to share the AI tools they’ve discovered that have helped, or could potentially help, during our weekly demo days. It’s a valuable exchange of ideas—for example, customer service reps advising designers on how to better program help chatbots.

Experts have observed the power of peer-to-peer learning networks, where employees develop and share ideas for AI adoption. Take an article in Harvard Business Review about AI usage at the European bank BBVA: “Instead of relying on the core IT and operations functions, the organization empowered the people who understood business processes best to design the solutions.”

While leaders can create a framework for AI adoption, starting with clear business priorities, they also need to tap employees for their ideas and insights into where and how tools can truly improve internal processes and the customer experience. Whether it’s an online forum, a Slack conversation, or a weekly all-hands meeting, make sure there’s a channel where employees can contribute their perspectives on AI development and share best practices. 

Make trade-offs deliberately

Organization-wide change requires investments of both time and money. That’s why I recommend encouraging employees to build slack into their schedules to test and experiment with new tools and figure out how to streamline their workflows. Each step eliminated, each minute of busywork recaptured makes a difference—and the benefits compound over time.

Recognizing that every AI initiative competes for limited time, budget, and attention helps organizations decide where to invest more wisely. Experts recommend managing AI investments like a portfolio, evaluating each one against objective criteria. Consider whether an investment serves broader business goals, whether additional training is needed, what other resources are required, and the cost of diverting those resources. As they assess potential investments, leaders can also track whether their overall AI strategy is delivering returns. As noted in another HBR article, “The goal is to ensure that individual projects advance business strategy and that the overall mix of investments creates sustainable value.”

Ultimately, this means being as deliberate about what to deprioritize as what to pursue. Success with AI depends less on which tools companies adopt and more on their willingness to stay focused on the initiatives that matter most. Be lazy about how much you take on, and smart about what you choose.

#10351. How to clock out psychologically—and leave the bad vibes at work

It’s hard to leave work stress where it belongs: at work. 

Stressful days spent navigating tense conversations with coworkers or clients, or staring down an endless to-do list or email queue, can cause rumination, anxiety, and even after-hours work. Your job anxiety can easily, and frequently, spill into your personal life.

To break the cycle, experts suggest creating a wind-down routine.

Understanding Emotional Residue and Rumination

Our brains are hardwired to replay unfinished business, which is why you can’t just turn off your thoughts after a tough day at work. Forcing yourself to stop thinking about a stressful situation usually backfires, and this can exacerbate your worry. 

“Trying not to think about it, generally does not work, as our brains will latch harder onto anything we’re trying to push out,” notes psychologist Meera Khan, clinical director at the mental health treatment company LifeStance Health in Bensalem, Pennsylvania.

Without a solid routine to wrap up your workday, spillover stress easily creeps into dinner time and ruins the rest of your night, according to the Journal of Occupational Health Psychology.

“When something upsetting happens at work, the stress doesn’t automatically disappear just because the workday is over,” explains neuropsychologist Sanam Hafeez, director of the neuropsychological assessment practice Comprehend the Mind in New York. “Your mind will oftentimes replay the moment over and over, trying to make sense of what happened,” she says. 

To break free from that mental loop, research published in the journal Acta Psychologica highlights a few simple strategies: First, acknowledge how you are feeling. Then, write it down or talk it through with someone. Finally, give yourself permission to step away and leave whatever is unfinished for tomorrow.

Simple Routines to Help You Unwind After Work

Having a noticeable routine at the end of the day signals your brain that work is over. Heading home used to give us a natural break, but working from home doesn’t give the same type of break. 

“Commuting is stressful, and it often means packed buses and standing in traffic,” points out Manuela Collis, assistant professor of organization and strategy at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College in Pittsburgh. “But the commute also did something useful for us: It created a temporal and physical boundary between what happens at work and life outside of it,” she says.

If there’s no commute, create new ways to wind down on your next WFH day. Stroll outside for a few minutes, walk your dog, or listen to an audiobook or podcast.

And then, after you log off, instead of dwelling on work issues all night, set a firm cutoff point and shift your focus to your personal life. “I recommend taking a few minutes at the end of each workday to write down anything that’s bothering you—that way, you have a clear plan for what to tackle the next day,” suggests Hafeez, who has a PsyD degree in school-community psychology.

Another tactic is to create a buffer. Before signing off, take two minutes to write down any worrisome tasks or stressors so they don’t linger in your head all night; putting something on paper can help transition it out of your mind, at least for now. Here are a few other simple ways to bridge the gap between work and your personal time.

  • Change your outfit: Take off your work clothes and put on comfy clothing. 
  • Take a 10-minute walk: Unplug, step away from your screen, and get some fresh air. 
  • Don’t feel compelled to check email: This one can be hard, given our 24/7 availability and smartphone culture—but the messages will be there tomorrow. So step away for tonight. 

The science backs this up. Per a study published in Frontiers in Psychology, participants who use such “sensory transition rituals” reduce work-life conflict by nearly half compared with those who are constantly on their devices. 

And if work stress still manages to sneak back in, it could be helpful to give yourself a finite time to worry.

“If you find yourself replaying work stress after hours, ask yourself if the issue is something you can solve right now,” advises Khan, who has a PsyD degree in clinical psychology. “I recommend a simple five-to-10-minute rule: If you can address it in five to 10 minutes, go ahead and do it. If not, let it wait,” she says.

Setting Boundaries and Normalizing Recovery Culture

As you make the shifts necessary to preserve your health and mental wellness, don’t feel guilty about it. This is time to reclaim your evenings and set boundaries. And when you work remotely, these blurred lines can make it a wee more challenging—especially given our culture of workaholism—but not impossible. 

“Working from home can make it feel like you’re expected to be available all the time,” Hafeez says. “But being a good employee doesn’t mean you have to be available 24/7.” Physical boundaries matter just as much as mental ones. “If you have the space or privilege to set up a dedicated workspace, try to keep all work-related activities contained to that area,” Khan suggests.

Leadership plays a key role, too. Managers need to practice what they preach and show their teams that staying online around the clock isn’t a badge of honor. 

“To help teams truly disconnect, managers can avoid scheduling late-day meetings, queue emails to send during regular working hours, and be crystal clear about expectations—especially what isn’t expected,” Collis notes.

The Bottom Line

The bad vibes shouldn’t follow you home; it’s okay to want to have calm evenings. Everyone is telling us to be more mindful and to preserve our headspace, but it isn’t an easy proposition. Clocking out from your work isn’t just about closing your laptop; it’s about creating meaningful and impactful ways to disconnect from work and keep tomorrow out of tonight.

#10350. Introducing AnyLanguageModel: One API for Local and Remote LLMs on Apple Platforms

LLMs have become essential tools for building software. But for Apple developers, integrating them remains unnecessarily painful.

Developers building AI-powered apps typically take a hybrid approach, adopting some combination of:

Each comes with different APIs, different requirements, different integration patterns. It's a lot, and it adds up quickly. When I interviewed developers about building AI-powered apps, friction with model integration came up immediately. One developer put it bluntly:

I thought I'd quickly use the demo for a test and maybe a quick and dirty build but instead wasted so much time. Drove me nuts.

The cost to experiment is high, which discourages developers from discovering that local, open-source models might actually work great for their use case.

Today we're announcing AnyLanguageModel, a Swift package that provides a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework with support for multiple model providers. Our goal is to reduce the friction of working with LLMs on Apple platforms and make it easier to adopt open-source models that run locally.

The core idea is simple: Swap your import statement, keep the same API.

Here's what that looks like in practice. Start with Apple's built-in model:

Now try an open-source model running locally via MLX:

AnyLanguageModel supports a range of providers:

The focus is on local models that you can download from the Hugging Face Hub. Cloud providers are included to lower the barrier to getting started and to provide a migration path. Make it work, then make it right.

When designing AnyLanguageModel, we faced a choice: create a new abstraction that tries to capture everything, or build on an existing API. We chose the latter, using Apple's Foundation Models framework as the template.

This might seem counterintuitive. Why tie ourselves to Apple's choices? A few reasons:

Foundation Models is genuinely well-designed. It leverages Swift features like macros for an ergonomic developer experience, and its abstractions around sessions, tools, and generation map well to how LLMs actually work.

It's intentionally limited. Foundation Models represents something like a lowest common denominator for language model capabilities. Rather than seeing this as a weakness, we treat it as a stable foundation (hyuk hyuk). Every Swift developer targeting Apple platforms will encounter this API, so building on it directly means less conceptual overhead.

It keeps us grounded. Each additional layer of abstraction takes you further from the problem you're actually solving. Abstractions are powerful, but stack too many and they become a problem in themselves.

The result is that switching between providers requires minimal code changes, and the core abstractions remain clean and predictable.

One challenge with multi-backend libraries is dependency bloat. If you only want to run MLX models, you shouldn't have to pull in llama.cpp and all its dependencies.

AnyLanguageModel uses Swift 6.1 package traits to solve this. You opt in to only the backends you need:

Available traits include CoreML, MLX, and Llama (for llama.cpp / llama.swift). By default, no heavy dependencies are included. You get the base API plus cloud providers, which only require standard URLSession networking.

For Xcode projects (which don't yet support trait declarations directly), you can create a small internal Swift package that depends on AnyLanguageModel with the traits you need, then add that package as a local dependency. The README has detailed instructions.

Vision-language models are incredibly capable and widely used. They can describe images, extract text from screenshots, analyze charts, and answer questions about visual content. Unfortunately, Apple's Foundation Models framework doesn't currently support sending images with prompts.

Building on an existing API means accepting its constraints. Apple will likely add image support in a future release (iOS 27, perhaps?), but vision-language models are too useful to wait for. So we've extended beyond what Foundation Models offers today.

Here's an example sending an image to Claude:

We're taking a calculated risk here; we might design something that conflicts with Apple's eventual implementation. But that's what deprecation warnings are for. Sometimes you have to write the API for the framework that doesn't exist yet.

To see AnyLanguageModel in action, check out chat-ui-swift, a SwiftUI chat application that demonstrates the library's capabilities.

It's meant as a starting point: Fork it, extend it, swap in different models. See how the pieces fit together and adapt it to your needs.

AnyLanguageModel is currently pre-1.0. The core API is stable, but we're actively working on bringing the full feature set of Foundation Models to all adapters, namely:

This library is the first step toward something larger. A unified inference API provides the scaffolding needed to build seamless agentic workflows on Apple platforms — applications where models can use tools, access system resources, and accomplish complex tasks. More on that soon. 🤫

#10349. Apple is turning your iPhone into a car key for 3 popular brands. Unlocking is only the beginning

Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC drivers will now be able to unlock their vehicles with their phones.

As first reported by MacRumors, General Motors announced that it has begun rolling out the Apple Wallet feature to select models. More vehicles are expected to be added over time. Eligible customers will receive notifications in the “What’s New” section of their vehicle’s app when digital-key support is available. 

Users will be able to use their smartphones or Apple Watches much like a physical key to unlock their vehicles. GM said supported vehicles will automatically unlock as a driver approaches and lock as the driver walks away. According to the company, the vehicle’s trunk and climate control system will be accessible with the new Apple Wallet feature. 

“The digital key experience will continue to evolve beyond simply unlocking and starting a vehicle. By leveraging ultra-wideband technology, GM is laying the groundwork for more deeply integrated and personalized experiences like automatically adjusting vehicle settings as drivers approach and other intelligent features that make ownership more convenient,” said the company in a press release.

Apple first announced the concept at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June 2020. It later launched exclusively for select 2021 BMW 5 Series models. Since then, the tech company has added other major automakers, such as Mercedes-Benz, Hyundai, Kia, Genesis, and Audi, to the offering.

The digital key may work even when a phone’s battery is dead. The company said that depending on a user’s iPhone model, keys could still be available even when a device needs to be charged. However, it warned that they will be available only for up to five hours.

The evolution of digital keys

Samsung rolled out its own version of the digital keys in 2021. In October, Samsung announced it would support digital keys for select GM vehicles. 

The digital key is the latest evolution in car-key technology. In the 1980s, automakers began using radio frequencies to create remote keyless entry fobs. 

In 2008, Nissan and tech company Sharp launched a mobile phone with a built-in intelligent car-key chip in Japan. Then, in 2017, Tesla advanced the concept by making its smartphone app the primary, default key for the Model 3, replacing the standard physical key fob. 

Apple and GM did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

#10347. Open ASR Leaderboard: Trends and Insights with New Multilingual & Long-Form Tracks

While everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up new ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show. As of 21 Nov 2025, there are 150 Audio-Text-to-Text and 27K ASR models on the Hub 🤯

Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.

Over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency. Recently, multilingual and long-form transcription tracks have been added to the leaderboard 🎉

As of 21 Nov 2025, the Open ASR Leaderboard compares 60+ open and closed-source models from 18 organizations, across 11 datasets.

In a recent preprint, we dive into the technical setup and highlight some key trends in modern ASR. Here are the big takeaways 👇

Models combining Conformer encoders with large language model (LLM) decoders currently lead in English transcription accuracy. For example, NVIDIA’s Canary-Qwen-2.5B, IBM’s Granite-Speech-3.3-8B, and Microsoft’s Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct achieve the lowest word error rates (WER), showing that integrating LLM reasoning can significantly boost ASR accuracy.

💡 Pro-tip: NVIDIA introduced Fast Conformer, a 2x faster variant of the Conformer, that is used in their Canary and Parakeet suite of models.

While highly accurate, these LLM decoders tend to be slower than simpler approaches. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, efficiency is measured using inverse real-time factor (RTFx), where higher is better.

For even faster inference, CTC and TDT decoders deliver 10–100× faster throughput, albeit with slightly higher error rates. This makes them ideal for real-time, offline, or batch transcription tasks (such as meetings, lectures, or podcasts).

OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 remains a strong multilingual baseline, supporting 99 languages. However, fine-tuned or distilled variants like Distil-Whisper and CrisperWhisper often outperform the original on English-only tasks, showing how targeted fine-tuning can improve specialization (how to fine-tune? Check out guides for Whisper, Parakeet, and Voxtral).

That said, focusing on English tends to reduce multilingual coverage 👉 a classic case of the tradeoff between specialization and generalization. Similarly, while self-supervised systems like Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) and Omnilingual ASR can support 1K+ languages, they trail behind language-specific encoders in accuracy.

⭐ While just five languages are currently benchmarked, we’re planning to expand to more languages and are excited for new dataset and models contributions to multilingual ASR through GitHub pull requests.

🎯 Alongside multilingual benchmarks, several community-driven leaderboards focus on individual languages. For example, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard compares models across Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, highlighting how speech variation and diglossia challenge current systems. Similarly. the Russian ASR Leaderboard provides a growing hub for evaluating encoder-decoder and CTC models on Russian-specific phonology and morphology. These localized efforts mirror the broader multilingual leaderboard’s mission to encourage dataset sharing, fine-tuned checkpoints, and transparent model comparisons, especially in languages with fewer established ASR resources.

For long-form audio (e.g., podcasts, lectures, meetings), closed-source systems still edge out open ones. It could be due to domain tuning, custom chunking, or production-grade optimization.

Among open models, OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 performs the best. But for throughput, CTC-based Conformers shine 👉 for example, NVIDIA’s Parakeet CTC 1.1B achieves an RTFx of 2793.75, compared to 68.56 for Whisper Large v3, with only a moderate WER degradation (6.68 and 6.43 respectively).

The tradeoff? Parakeet is English-only, again reminding us of that multilingual and specialization tradeoff 🫠.

⭐ While closed systems still lead, there’s huge potential for open-source innovation here. Long-form ASR remains one of the most exciting frontiers for the community to tackle next!

Given how fast ASR is evolving, we’re excited to see what new architectures push performance and efficiency, and how the Open ASR Leaderboard continues to serve as a transparent, community-driven benchmark for the field, and as a reference for other leaderboards (Russian, Arabic, and Speech DeepFake Detection).

We’ll keep expanding the Open ASR LeaderBoard with more models, more languages, and more datasets so stay tuned 👀

👉 Want to contribute? Head on over to the GitHub repo to open a pull request 🚀

#10346. The smartest AI might be the one that leaves us alone

One of the ideas I’m always trying to tell my students is that their brains are something, an asset, if you like, they need to protect. The human brain is an amazing optimizer: Provide it with an effortless way to achieve something, and it will quickly start to use it. We used to memorize a ton of phone numbers a few decades ago. Now we can hardly memorize our own, simply because our brain knows the number is a few clicks away. 

A clear example is why I never use AI to write my articles: simply because, for me, in my personal methodology as a professor of innovation, writing is my way of making concepts stick in my brain, concepts I will need later to teach and discuss. If I ask ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or any other chatbot to write my articles for me, I would lose much of the learning that writing gives me.

This doesn’t mean I don’t use AI: I can use it to translate certain parts, to search for relevant articles to back up an assertion, or to assess whether the concepts I try to explain come across clearly. But I don’t want to use it for writing, because writing is a skill I want to protect. And like a muscle, if you don’t exercise it, it quickly atrophies.

For a manager, the skill worth protecting might be decision-making: An AI that makes every choice could undermine precisely the judgment that person needs to develop. The useful behavior depends on the objective, and sometimes that objective requires the system to hold back. 

What happens when we move from personal to corporate use? Can an AI learn when its intervention would make things worse? That capability might receive very little applause in a product demonstration, but it could be enormously valuable in practice.

The sales agent that lets us be 

Imagine a company using a sales agent. When it identifies a customer approaching renewal, it follows a standard procedure: It quickly reviews the account, writes a personalized email, offers a discount, and schedules a follow-up. All of it in mere seconds. And the audience claps enthusiastically. 

But what if our customer would have renewed anyway? Then, the end result is that we have wasted an interaction, risked alienating the customer, and surrendered margin unnecessarily. What if our customer is a happy one, and the right thing to do would have been just to wait for him or her to renew voluntarily? 

Even when all tasks are perfectly executed, the decision to perform them could have been perfectly wrong. 

The cost of being helpful

We know how this feels when we’re working with real people: Experienced employees often develop a sense of when to follow up, when to escalate an issue, and when making too many interventions will look messy, send the wrong signal, or make the customer upset. How do they know that? It comes with experience; it’s learning that compounds over time, with more and more iterations.

That judgment is something we pay to have. However, when we evaluate AI, we tend to be fascinated with visible activity—with messages generated, tasks completed, workflows executed, etc. The equivalent is if we were dealing with a hyperactive employee. And as we probably know, someone who sends twice the number of messages is probably not twice as valuable. 

In other words, just because an action can be automated and, therefore, performed easily, doesn’t mean that we should be performing it all the time. 

Look what happens with AI coding assistants: In “When to show a suggestion? Integrating human feedback in AI-assisted programming,” Microsoft researchers used data from 535 programmers to retrospectively evaluate a system that selectively withheld suggestions that were apparently likely to be rejected by the developers. They also found that optimizing for suggestion acceptance could produce lower-quality suggestions. Getting people to accept more assistance was an imperfect measure of helping them. 

Learning when to intervene

In the case of our renewal agent, a system that learns from a lot of comparable cases could perhaps investigate which interventions help with whom. For instance, some customers don’t like the feeling of being “directed” or “influenced,” and are better left to their own devices. Some like a particular type of interaction through a particular channel, but they hate others. Or they want to talk to the same customer representatives every time because they remember them. 

The function to protect would be the ability to spot these cases. Do not automate; optimize. But optimization is not necessarily something that today’s corporate AI does well. Today’s corporate AIs can generate splendid emails, but following the before and after and deciding to do nothing is usually not an alternative. 

It’s the experience from all previous cases, processed along with the specific characteristics of every customer, that leads to the lessons learned, to the continuous improvement, to the process being optimized. And that ability to improve decisions through accumulated experience is precisely what you need. 

Give waiting a fair chance

When buying or deploying AI, managers should, therefore, find out what outcome the system is theoretically trying to improve, and design ways to know whether its actions helped or not. We need to be honest here: A renewal following an email does not necessarily establish that the email was the reason for the renewal. Customers differ, circumstances change, and useful comparisons may require carefully designed experiments. Simply storing more interaction histories will not settle the question. 

This includes maintaining the necessary human oversight, the now-famous “human-in-the-loop”: A missed warning or an unanswered complaint can be costly. People must define the obligations and limits within which the system can learn. 

I haven’t seen an AI system that reviews an account, checks all the available evidence from the corporate ERP or CRM, and decides that contacting the customer would probably make things worse. So the final outcome would be that nothing gets sent, no discount is offered, and we just let the customer evolve naturally. No hyperactivity. Why? Because our corporate learning optimized it, and the accumulated learning behind that decision should remain under our company’s control, available even if we replace the model or the vendor powering our agents.

It might be a disappointing demo. But it could be excellent business.
