#10330. Building Deep Research: How we Achieved State of the Art

Research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most important applications of AI. Research is a foundational knowledge-work task: collecting, reading, and synthesizing information underpins everything from writing and decision-making to coding itself. Yet human-driven research is constrained by memory, reading speed, and time. AI research agents, by contrast, can process vast amounts of information, synthesize insights instantly, and scale effortlessly. Because of this, research agents are emerging as a top use case for AI today and will soon become a core subcomponent of broader agentic workflows across content generation, coding, sales, and more. In this post, we share the technical and philosophical lessons we’ve learned building a state-of-the-art research agent, and where we believe the field is headed.

The task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling. Building applications on top of rapidly improving models is, however, a modern engineering challenge. How can we design software today that absorbs the performance gains from future model releases?

This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.

We learned this the hard way seven months ago, when we had to abandon our first attempt at deep research and rebuild the entire system from scratch. The first architecture was complicated and sophisticated (we thought this was a good thing), but its assumptions became bottlenecks when the next generation of models arrived.

Over the last seven months, model capabilities have quietly but meaningfully evolved (especially in their tool-calling abilities). This single optimization focus has pushed us from workflows to agents. We believe future models will be trained to solve the current pain points of agent developers. Every model is ultimately consumed by a harness, so models should evolve in service of that harness. We hope to see models improve in high-recall summarization (for context compression), tool-calling reliability, and concision in writing.

Similarly, tools should evolve to support LLMs and widely adopted agent harnesses. The best tools should perform some context engineering on the tool side, abstracted away from the agent. They should return only the most relevant data instead of dumping large volumes of tokens into the context window. As a tool provider, we’ve invested heavily in our advanced search feature, which has context engineering baked in. This in turn lowers hallucinations and latency for the downstream agent processes.

To build agents that improve over time, we followed a few guiding principles:

Long-horizon research tasks expose a fundamental challenge in current agent design: the task of maintaining a clean, optimized context window over time. If curating context is not a task the engineer pays close attention to, the agent is almost destined for failure. The following outlines our thinking around this concept within the deep research domain.

Using Tavily’s Advanced Search is the natural first step to take in overcoming this challenge, in that it abstracts away the processing of raw web content and returns only the most relevant content chunks from each source. In leveraging this functionality, we let Tavily Search do the heavy lifting and allow Tavily Research to reap the benefit, gathering the most valuable content in a latency-efficient manner.

Ensuring that the agent does not overfit to a single research thread is the next step towards an effective context-gathering pipeline. It is in this regard that global state persistence and source deduplication is paramount, and in our case, it helps threefold:

At Tavily, interacting with the web is our bread and butter. Architecting a refined web-retrieval system engineered for deep research was a foundational building block for our deep research agent design as a whole.

Humans research in an inherently unstructured, iterative way. We start by defining the task: what we’re trying to accomplish and what information we need. We next gather data from our sources, extracting the key insights and holding them in short-term memory, letting these distilled thoughts guide our subsequent actions.

This cycle repeats: collect information, distill it, decide what to do next. Only once we’ve gathered enough understanding to produce the final deliverable do we return to the original sources, using them as references to assemble the finished product.

We believe that deep research agents should be designed in a similar manner, in that tool outputs should be distilled into reflections, and only the set of past reflections should be used as context for your tool caller. Similar to humans, it is only at the point when your agent begins to prepare the final deliverable that you must provide the raw information as context, so as to ensure there is no information loss.

This approach differs from traditional context structuring in a ReAct agent-based architecture. Typically, tool calls and outputs are propagated through the tool calling loop, with previously retrieved/generated tokens being persisted in the context window on each subsequent iteration. This pattern can be seen in LangChain’s Open Deep Research agent implementation, and from a token consumption perspective, it can be modeled by the following quadratic series, where n n n is the amount of tokens the tool calling model is invoked with on each tool calling iteration, and m m m is the number of tool calling iterations.

n+2n+3n+⋯+mn  =  n⋅m(m+1)2n + 2n + 3n + \cdots + mn \;=\; n \cdot \frac{m(m+1)}{2}n+2n+3n+⋯+mn=n⋅2m(m+1)​

Contrarily, our proposed method of context engineering removes this token propagation (as the knowledge distillations, even when aggregated, are negligible when compared to the quantity of tokens gathered from web) and can be modeled by the following linear series.

n+n+n+⋯+n  =  nmn + n + n + \cdots + n \;=\; nmn+n+n+⋯+n=nm

When comparing the two approaches, tokens are saved on a per-agent basis by a factor of m+12 \frac{m+1}{2} 2m+1​, and when extrapolating this over a multi-agent system and with consumption at scale, the absolute value of tokens saved becomes even more significant.

Through this methodology, we were able to reduce token consumption by 66% (when compared to Open Deep Research) while achieving SOTA on DeepResearch Bench – the intersection of quality and efficiency in full effect.

Building production-grade agents is a balancing act. We leaned into autonomy to maximize performance and quality, while still meeting strict requirements for latency, cost, and reliability.

LLMs are inherently non-deterministic, and we found that giving them guard-railed freedom to reason and iterate produces the strongest results. Autonomy, when gone wrong, can cause agent behavior to go off track. Tools can be called incorrectly, LLMs can overfit to a subtopic, and expected reasoning patterns may break. No single safeguard will catch all of these issues.

A shift in engineering mindset is required: treat failure modes as core design considerations, not afterthoughts. Simple guardrails like tool-call retries or model cascades help, but proactively anticipating anomalies, reinforcing proper patterns in prompting and edge-case testing is what enables production-grade, long-running agents.

From our experience, it’s better to expose a small, essential toolset to the agent rather than a large, complex one. We were tempted to over-engineer by adding many tools that seemed useful in theory, but in practice this created new failure modes and made it harder for LLMs to consistently choose the right tool and iterate effectively.

We used evals to steer our development process but also recognize their shortcomings. LLM-as-a-judge evals are difficult to trust: current models are non‑deterministic, uninterpretable in their reasoning, and can turn into bottlenecks, especially for long‑running agents where a single experiment can take days to complete.

Rather than optimizing for benchmark scores, we optimized for directional feedback. The core question was always: did this change make the agent more reliable and more useful in practice? Evals became a tool for validating that direction, not the optimization target. Intuition and careful agent‑trace monitoring consistently provided higher‑signal feedback than any single eval score. Overall, the best outcome is rarely the highest numerical score. For production systems, improvements like reduced token usage, reliability, lower latency, and fewer failures are more valuable than a one‑point bump on an eval.

If you’re interested in experiencing the result of these findings in practice, you can sign up for early access to Tavily Research here.

When we decompile these files (called APKs, in the case of Android apps), we’re able to see various lines of code within that hint at possible future features. Keep in mind that Google may or may not ever ship these features, and our interpretation of what they are may be imperfect. We’ll try to enable those that are closer to being finished, however, to show you how they’ll look in case that they do ship. With that in mind, read on.

Google Voice for Android version 2026.11.01.1014278023 doesn’t enable RCS, but it does, for the first time, actually hint that the functionality might be on its way. In a teardown of the app, one simple string stands out:

That points to a new send button used for RCS messages rather than SMS. Google Messages similarly changes its send button to differentiate between the two standards.

Google has been championing RCS support for over a decade now, so it’s long past due for Voice, a long-running Google product, to get on board. While the tidbits in this update don’t serve as any confirmation RCS if coming to Voice, it’s the most exciting update on the matter in years.

#10328. This new scorecard shows whether your favorite retailer is using Flock cameras

Automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and other vendors have become increasingly controversial across the country after reports of misuse by officers, high error rates that can lead to dangerous police encounters, and concerns about access by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.  

Flock, in particular, operates a nationwide camera network, with data from cameras operated in one jurisdiction frequently accessed by investigators from elsewhere, making it hard for local officials to understand and control privacy risks. As a result, while Flock and other providers emphasize that their cameras have been used to investigate legitimate crimes, rescue kidnapped kids, and track stolen cars, many municipalities have ended their contracts, in some cases even covering cameras awaiting removal by the service provider.   

Many businesses deploy their own automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, to track vehicles in their parking lots, sometimes sharing that information with law enforcement. But since private companies aren’t subject to freedom of information laws, it can be hard to know which businesses have them and what they’re doing with the data they collect.

To help people understand in time for the holiday shopping season which stores use the devices, Fight for the Future just released a scorecard listing 10 major retailers and what the organization knows about their use of the cameras.  

“Retailers also need to be brought into the conversation,” says Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at Fight for the Future, which previously organized a campaign with home improvement influencers that called on Home Depot and Lowe’s to cut ties with Flock.

The chart is based on information the organization received from a questionnaire sent to the retailers and, in cases where they didn’t respond, third-party news reporting, crowdsourced camera spotting, and information from published privacy policies. “We got responses from just a handful of [businesses],” Suleiman says.  

The exact details vary, and many businesses don’t appear to use the technology at every location. Costco, for instance, told Fight for the Future that it uses ALPR cameras at “less than a dozen locations nationwide,” so it’s difficult to know just from the checklist whether your local branch of a national chain is equipped with the cameras.

But it’s easy to see at a glance that many major brands at least acknowledge in their privacy policies that they might be using the technology. Some stores also indicate that they may share information from the devices with law enforcement. 

The scorecard offers links to retailers’ emails, along with suggested text, to ask them to refrain from using ALPR technology, even if (or perhaps especially if) the details about how they do so may be opaque. Fight for the Future also encourages people to reach out with any tips about retailers that are using the cameras or with requests to add particular stores to the scoresheet. 

“We don’t have a FOIA request that we can do for companies or a public records act request that we can impose upon companies, but nothing’s stopping us from writing to them,” Suleiman says. “Nothing’s stopping people from letting these companies know what they want and what they expect.”

#10326. Continuous batching from first principles

TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.

If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency. That's because at the heart of it, all LLMs are just fancy next token predictors. An LLM first processes your entire prompt to produce one new token. Then it keeps adding tokens one by one, each time reading everything that came before, until it decides generation is over.

This generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated. To make these models practical for real-world applications, particularly when serving many users simultaneously, researchers and engineers have developed a range of efficient inference techniques.One of the most impactful optimizations is continuous batching, which attempts to maximize performance by processing multiple conversations in parallel and swapping them out when they are done.

To understand how continuous batching works and why it's so effective in high-load serving scenarios, we'll build up from the fundamentals of how LLMs process tokens.

The attention mechanism is the central piece of how LLMs work. A language model processes text by breaking it down into pieces that we call tokens. We can conceptually think of "tokens" as "words", but sometimes a word might be composed of several tokens. For each token sequence, the network computes a prediction of what the next token should be.

Many operations in the network are token-wise: each token is processed independently, and the output for a given token depends only on that token's content, not on any other tokens in the sequence. Operations like this include layer normalization or matrix multiplication. However, to create connections between words in a sentence, we need operations where tokens can influence each other.

This is where attention comes in. Attention layers are the only place where different tokens interact with each other. Understanding how a network connects tokens together means understanding attention.

Let's see how this works in practice, in the case where there is only one input prompt.

Consider the initial prompt I am sure this project, tokenized as 7 tokens: [, I, am, sure, this, pro, ject]. The , or "Beginning of Sequence", is a special token we add at the start of the prompt to tell the language model that a new conversation starts here.

Each token is represented inside the network with a vector of length d (the hidden dimension). Therefore, the seven incoming tokens form a tensor xxx with shape [1,7,d]\left[1, 7, d \right][1,7,d]. 1 is the number of sequences, or batch size, which is just one in our case. 7 is the sequence length, and d is the hidden dimension, or the size of each token representation. Going forward, we'll use nnn instead of 7 as the sequence length.

Input tensor x x x is then projected by three matrices: the query projection Wq W_q Wq​, the key projection Wk W_k Wk​ and the value projection Wv W_v Wv​. This produces three tensors Q Q Q, K K K and V V V, all of shape [1,n,A] \left[1, n , A \right] [1,n,A], where A A A is the dimension of the attention head. We call them the query, key and value states, respectively. This is represented on the left in the figure below.

Next, tensors Q Q Q and K K K are multiplied together to measure similarity between tokens, producing a tensor of shape [1,n,n] \left[ 1, n , n \right] [1,n,n]. This is why we say that attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length. Computing QKT QK^T QKT requires O(n2d) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 d \right) O(n2d) operations, so the cost is a square of n n n the sequence length. It is represented on the right in the figure above.

We then apply a boolean attention mask to QKT QK^T QKT to control which tokens can interact, as represented in the figure below. In this figure, the attention mask is a causal mask, meaning each token only interacts with tokens that came before it. This follows the intuition that a cause must come before its consequence, hence the name causal mask. The attention mask is crucial because it dictates all token interactions in the network. Set all attention mask values to False and no token will ever interact with another in the whole network. We'll examine attention masks more closely in a few paragraphs.

Finally, after applying the attention mask, we take a token-wise softmax (which is the same as saying a row-wise softmax) and multiply the result by the value projection V V V to get the output of one attention head, of shape [1,n,A] \left[ 1, n , A \right] [1,n,A]. We offer a visual summary of the whole process in the following figure.

We are going to use a lot of attention visualization in this post, so to simplify things, we are going to condense the figure above just a bit.

Why this matters: In continuous batching, Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V can have different numbers of tokens because, as we'll see, we'll be processing different stages (prefill and decode) at the same time. To make it more general, let's say Q Q Q has shape [1,nQ,A] \left[1, n_Q , A \right] [1,nQ​,A], K K K has shape [1,nK,A] \left[ 1, n_K , A \right] [1,nK​,A], and V V V has shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A].

The attention scores QKT QK^T QKT then have shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​], and the attention mask has the same shape since it's applied point-wise to the scores.

After applying the attention mask and row-wise softmax, we multiply by V V V. Since we're multiplying a matrix of shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​] by one of shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A], the inner dimensions must match: nK=nV n_K = n_V nK​=nV​. This means V V V and K K K always have the same length, so we can simplify our visualizations by only showing K K K.Don't worry if this seems abstract: the figures will make it concrete.

Furthermore, since we know that the attention mask is applied to QKT QK^T QKT, we know they have the same shape. Instead of representing the attention scores, we will represent the attention mask in its place. Finally, since Q Q Q, K K K and V V V are direct projections of x x x, no need to represent x x x. This gives the simplified figure where we only represent Q Q Q, K K K and the attention mask:

This representation also underlines how we can read an attention mask.

We read the mask row-by-row, which is the same as reading token-by-token: each row corresponds to one token's attention computation. A green square at position (row i, column j) means True: token j can influence token i. A white square means False: no interaction allowed.

For example, look at the third row for token "am". The "I" column is green, so "I" influences the computation of "am". The "pro" column is white, so "pro" doesn't influence "am" . This is causal masking at work: future tokens can't affect past ones.

The last layer of the model outputs a token prediction for each input token. In our context, generating the continuation of a single prompt, we only care about the next token prediction from the last token. The last token is "ject" in the figure above, and the associated prediction is "will".

The process we just described, where we take an entire input sequence, pass it through multiple attention layers and compute a score for the next token, is called prefill. This is because, as we'll see in a moment, much of the computation we performed can be cached and reused – hence, we are prefilling the cache. Thanks to the use of this cache, sequence generation can proceed using much less compute in a phase called decoding. In the decoding phase, generating one new token will be much faster than the initial full-sequence computation. Let's see why.

To continue generation, we begin a new forward pass, which would naively look like this:

To compute the attention scores of the new token, we still need the key and value projections of the previous tokens. So we need to repeat the matrix multiplication of the old tokens (in grey in the figure above) with Wk W_k Wk​ and Wv W_v Wv​ to retrieve a result that was already computed once before. In other terms, we are wasting compute. Let's see how we can avoid that.

Right off the bat, we notice that the last token does not impact the attention calculation of the other tokens:

This follows the idea of the causal mask: since "will" comes after all previous tokens, it does not change their attention calculation. For text generation, causal attention is by far the most common, so we will focus on that case from now on. Keep in mind that non-causal attention schemes can also be used, especially when dealing with images. Considering we only need the next-token prediction for the "will" token, we can simplify the attention mechanism by only computing the output for this token.

Moreover, we already computed the K K K and V V V states for the tokens "", … , "ject" during the previous forward pass: if they have been stored, we do not need to recompute them again. This is the KV cache: the list of key and value states created during generation. It essentially allows one to reduce the compute cost of generating token n+1 n+1 n+1 from O(n2) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 \right) O(n2) to O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n) by avoiding recomputation of key and value projections, while paying a memory cost of O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n).

In the figure above, only the tokens in white are computed: instead of computing the keys and values for 8 tokens, we compute them for 1. You can see that through KV caching, a lot of compute is saved.You can check this post for more visualizations of KV caching, or this one for a practical implementation example.

Let's be a bit more specific about the cache size, because it's a good opportunity to examine the shapes present in our model. For a model with L \mathcal L L attention layers and H H H attention heads with head dimension A A A, the total cache size needed to store one token will be 2∗L∗AH 2 *\mathcal L * AH 2∗L∗AH with a factor of 2 2 2 to account for both K K K and V V V.For instance, Llama-2-7B with L=32 \mathcal{L}=32 L=32 layers, H=32 H=32 H=32 heads, and A=128 A=128 A=128 requires 2×32×128=8,192 2 \times 32 \times 128 = 8,192 2×32×128=8,192 values per token per layer. With float16 precision, this takes 2AH×2 2AH \times 2 2AH×2 bytes =16 = 16 =16 KB in memory.

KV caching is useful when we want to generate the next token, which is a stage we call decoding. But it can also be useful in the prefill stage, when we process the initial prompt and have many input tokens. Especially when there are large initial prompts that don't fit in GPU memory all at once.

Up till now, we have looked at an example of prefill where we have n=7 n=7 n=7 tokens, but in practice initial prompts can be much longer. For instance, when using Cursor, you can add your repository to the prompt, where it acts as context: this significantly increases the prompt size. In such cases, the memory needed to store the activations for n n n tokens can be larger than the available memory on the GPU. Thus we cannot perform prefill in a single forward pass: we have to split the prefill in chunks. This is called chunked prefill, and it's going to be one of the components needed to enable efficient inference.

Let's pretend that the available memory is very constrained, and that we can only pass m=4 m=4 m=4 tokens per forward pass. If we have an initial prompt with n=7 n = 7 n=7 tokens, we need to split it in ⌈n/m⌉=2 \lceil n /m \rceil = 2 ⌈n/m⌉=2 chunks (rounding up 7/4 = 1.75 to 2). We illustrate the example below using the same n n n and m m m notations:

We can do that thanks to the KV cache. We store the KV states during the first prefill split, and during the second prefill split, we prepend the stored KV states to the new KV states. We also adapt the attention mask accordingly. Visually, it looks like we split the non-chunked prefill in the middle.

The key insight: cached KV states let us process the prompt incrementally without losing information.

Although we showed here an example where we split the prefill into 2 chunks, chunked prefill can be used to split the prefill in any way we want, adapting flexibly to memory constraints.

We are now finally equipped with all the tools we need to understand Continuous Batching.

In our previous examples we have only considered the case of batch size one, i.e. we only generate tokens for one prompt at a time. In the context of evaluation or model serving, we want to generate tokens for a large number of prompts. To increase the throughput, which is the number of tokens generated per second, the best course of action is to generate tokens in parallel for a batch of several prompts.

To batch prompts together, the naive way is to add an axis to both input tensors: token sequence and attention mask. However, this comes with a constraint on the shape of the inputs: we need all prompts to have the same length, because tensors must be rectangular. To achieve this, we usually add padding on the left so the new token prediction always comes from the rightmost token. We also modify the attention mask of each prompt accordingly, as shown below:

where the padding tokens are coloured in orange. Then we can perform the forward pass as we used to, with the added dimension of the batch size. This is called batched generation: efficient for same-length prompts, but wasteful when lengths vary.It is illustrated below, through 4 steps of generation: one prefilling step (at the top) and 3 decoding steps (below each "Forward pass" lines).

where means "End Of Sequence", this is a special token to indicate the model has reached the end of generation for the corresponding sequence.

The drawback of batched generation is that if one prompt finishes generation before the other one by generating an token, all further generated tokens are useless. And this goes on until the longest request of the batch finishes. Of course, we can remove the prompts that have reached an token from the batch and save some compute and memory, but saving resources is not the goal here: throughput is.

Instead of just removing the finished prompt from the batch, we can replace it with a prompt that's waiting for generation. We will call this dynamic scheduling, or dynamic batching. Dynamic scheduling is great to maintain throughput while ensuring any token generated by a forward pass is relevant. But because of the way we batched prompts together, it has a major drawback: we need a lot of padding when swapping prompts. That's because the newly-inserted prompt needs to go through prefill while the other prompts are decoding one token at a time. So there is almost as much padding as there are tokens in the newly-inserted prompt.

The problem becomes even worse when batch size increases and initial prompts are long. The padding cost grows quadratically with both batch size and prompt length. If we have a batch of B B B prompts that are in decoding phase and one finishes, dynamically introducing a prompt of n n n initial tokens in the batch requires (n−1)(B−1) (n-1)(B-1) (n−1)(B−1) padding tokens. For instance, with B=8 B=8 B=8 and n=100 n=100 n=100, we'd need 99×7=693 99 \times 7 = 693 99×7=693 padding tokens!

Furthermore, practical optimizations like CUDA graphs or torch.compile require static tensor shapes. This forces us to pad all prompts to a fixed maximum length, dramatically increasing the padding waste.

At this point, our main problem is padding, which is a consequence of the axis we added to batch sentences together. Thus, the ideal would be to get rid of this axis entirely, a radical rethinking of batching. If we do so, the only way to batch prompts together is to concatenate them:

But we don't want tokens from prompt 0 to interact with the tokens of prompt 1! Luckily for us, we have a way to control how tokens interact with one another: the attention mask. How we do this is displayed below:

Although we use different tints of green to illustrate the different parts of the attention mask, this is still a boolean mask with only greens for True and white for False. This way of batching prompts together is called ragged batching (because sequence lengths are 'ragged' or uneven), and it offers the benefit of added throughput without introducing the need for padding tokens.

In the figure above, we use ragged batching to combine two full prompts together, but we can batch as many as memory allows. The only limit is m m m, the number of tokens we can fit in a batch, with m m m depending on the available memory on the GPU.

Ragged batching is one of the key components of continuous batching. To maximize throughput, we can combine prefill and decoding sequences following an algorithm like this:

Dynamic scheduling is the final piece that contributes to the continuous batching technique: we remove finished prompts from the batch as soon as they are done, and replace them with new chunked prompts that correspond to incoming requests.

This combination of ragged batching and dynamic scheduling is called continuous batching, and it's the technique that powers modern LLM serving systems.

Continuous batching combines three key techniques to maximize throughput in LLM serving:

By removing the batch dimension and using attention masks to control token interactions, continuous batching allows mixing prefill and decode phases in the same batch, dramatically improving efficiency for serving multiple requests. This is why services like ChatGPT can handle thousands of concurrent users efficiently.

In the next article in this series, we make continuous batching much more efficient by introducing asynchronous batching. Read it here!If you'd like to see a deep dive on other continuous batching topics, please let us know in the comments!

Thanks for the article! I'd like to add one note: the primary reason we need chunked prefill isn't the memory constraint (otherwise we could simply solve it with Flash Attention). The more practical reason is that a long prefill blocks all decode requests in the batch. Chunking it lets decode requests make progress between chunks. Moreover, since prefill chunks make the forward pass compute-bound, decode tokens can piggyback on the same batch at nearly zero marginal cost - they're just extra rows in an already large matmul. This turns memory-bound decode-only batches into better-utilized compute-saturating ones. See the SARATHI paper for details.

#10325. Gen Z is bringing back something retailers thought was dying

As consumers ready for the holiday season, it looks like gift shopping is taking a step away from the keyboard and moving back to brick-and-mortar locations.

According to research from Alchemer’s 2026 Holiday Shopper Report, more U.S. shoppers are planning to shop in physical retail stores. Some 35.8% say they will mainly shop in person, versus 31% who plan to shop mainly online.

But surprisingly, the revival of in-store shopping is being driven by a generation that mostly missed out on the mall’s heyday: Gen Z.

Research from the market research company Emarketer shows that around 51% of Gen Z are opting to shop in stores rather than online or on apps. Their preferences are showing up in spending, too. Shoppers aged 18 to 24 made 62% of their purchases in physical stores last year, compared with 52% of those 25 and older.

For Gen Z, a trip to a physical store is about more than just shopping. It’s an experience, and 63% of them say they bought something while there. The in-person shopping experience also has a social element to it. Nearly three in five Gen Z respondents say they shop as a way to spend time with others.

The clothing aisle is leading the way back to the store, as around one in five Gen Zers say they visit a clothing store every month, twice the rate of all adults.

Emarketer also found that many retailers are tapping into the renewed interest in real-world shopping, particularly catering to Gen Z. For instance, many are leaning on building community through in-store programming, like ornament making and letter-writing workshops at Macy’s, or fragrance readings at Lush, the personal care retailer.

A unifying trend across ages is a low tolerance for friction. Customers are looking for smooth shopping experiences. Alchemer’s survey found that shoppers are particularly sensitive to disruptions like slow checkouts and items being out of stock.

#10323. Target earnings: Retailer reports strong sales momentum ahead of the holidays as TGT stock soars in 2026

Retail giant Target Corporation (NYSE: TGT) has reported its third-quarter earnings for fiscal 2026, and they are a night-and-day difference compared to the results posted for the same quarter a year earlier.

Target’s sales growth for the period was the best in half a decade, suggesting that a turnaround plan from its new CEO is working. Here’s what you need to know.

Target’s Q3 2026 at a glance

This morning before the opening bell, Target reported its Q3 2026 earnings, a period that ended on October 31. By and large, the results were music to investors’ ears:

  • Net sales: $27.1 billion (up 7.1% YOY)
  • Adjusted earnings per share (EPS): $2.65 (up 74.8%)
  • Operating income: $1.67 billion (up 76.4%)
  • Net earnings: $1.21 billion (up 75.8%)

It should be noted that Target’s Q3 was helped somewhat by tariff refunds. During the quarter, the company received $301 million back through refunds.

Those refunds contributed $228 million to net earnings as well as 50 cents to the company’s earnings per share for the quarter.

Even so, Target handily beat analyst expectations on several fronts, notes CNBC. Analysts had expected revenue of $26.5 billion and an EPS of $2.07. Even after discounting the 50 cent EPS tariff boost, Target would still have topped analysts’ expectations on earnings per share by 8 cents.

Announcing the results, Target’s CEO, Michael Fiddelke, who took the helm in February and immediately launched a turnaround effort, said the company’s “third-quarter results reflect continued progress against our strategic priorities, centered on serving busy families with our signature blend of style, design and value.”

Target’s turnaround efforts appear to be working

A year ago, Target’s business looked much bleaker than it does today. The company was facing challenges on multiple fronts.

Many retailers at that time were also facing some of those same challenges: increased tariffs and customers cutting back on discretionary spending as inflationary pressure bit into their pocketbooks.

But Target was also facing a set of challenges unique to itself. Declining foot traffic had been driven by self-inflicted wounds over the years, including understaffed stores, messier merchandising, and DEI rollbacks that prompted a significant boycott of the company.

When Fiddelke took the reins in February, he sought to correct many of these issues, implementing sweeping changes, including a refined merchandising strategy that complemented Target’s strengths relative to competitors (such as well-designed home and apparel offerings). 

He also began remodeling stores to give them a new, modern look, and increased staffing at those stores to better meet customers’ needs.

Those changes appear to be working. Target says that in Q3, comparable foot traffic grew by 5%, while net sales grew 7.1% compared to last year. As CNBC noted, that’s Target’s best sales growth in more than five years.

TGT shares have soared in 2026

A strong Q3 has led Target to update its expectations for fiscal year 2026.

The company is now in its all-important Q4, which covers the end-of-year holiday period. For fiscal 2026, Target says it now expects full-year net sales growth in a range of around 6%, which is one point higher than the 5% the company initially forecast.

Still, despite the strong Q3 results, TGT shares are currently down about 1.1% in premarket trading, as of this writing.

Some of that may be attributed to profit-taking. Target’s stock price has surged by more than 60% this year, and investors often decide to lock in profits after a good quarter.

However, the drop in the company’s stock price may also signal investor concern about Target’s future business. There’s no doubt that Target was helped this quarter by its tariff refunds. But those refunds won’t keep coming forever.

Additionally, Target said it expects its capex to be between $5 billion and $6 billion in 2027. That is an increase of $1 billion from what Target spent in 2026.

While such spending may benefit Target in the long term, it can impact near-term growth, and investors generally think in the near term.

#10322. An Eric Trump-backed startup unveils a powerful new humanoid robot—and won’t rule out arming it

Foundation Future Industries, a startup backed by Eric Trump, has unveiled a humanoid robot that can carry 200 pounds while walking through rain, snow, and dust. The company wants its new Phantom MKII to work on construction sites and in factories—but the CEO isn’t ruling out putting weapons in its hands.

Sankaet Pathak, founder and CEO of Foundation, tells Fast Company his company would consider arming its machines if asked to by the U.S. military, arguing that deploying robots on the ground could reduce reliance on drones and air strikes.

“We’re not anti-weaponization and warfare,” he says. “That’s not something we have a blanket policy of just saying we’re not going to do.”

Phantom MKII is a second-generation humanoid designed for heavy industry and defense, unveiled today alongside Cortex II, the AI system that controls it. Foundation, which counts Eric Trump among its investors and advisers, has been particularly open about military applications—at times drawing controversy.

Earlier this month, the Financial Times reported that Foundation’s cofounder and president, Mike LeBlanc, was in direct talks with the Israel Defense Forces to supply up to 1,000 of its first-generation Phantom MKI robots for operations in tunnels beneath Gaza. Pathak disputes that characterization. “We’re not in talks with the IDF in any official capacity on deploying robots there,” he says. “What we have are very early exploration conversations.” When pressed about LeBlanc’s comments, Pathak says there is “literally nothing actively going on,” and there are no conversations progressing toward a contract.

Previously, Foundation said its machines had been tested with Ukrainian forces, while LeBlanc has described potential uses for them in detecting booby traps and trip wires.

For now, Pathak says most of Foundation’s defense work focuses on logistics rather than combat—though he doesn’t rule out deploying his machines on the battlefield. “Any time DOW [Department of War] will come to us and say, ‘Well, we need these robots more on the active battlefield with a weapon,’ to me that indicates that means less drones, less air strikes, more precision,” he says.

Pathak believes ground-based robots could accomplish military objectives without bombing entire buildings, potentially shortening wars.

Whether deployed in war or on construction sites, which Pathak sees as the robot’s ideal initial use, the Phantom MKII is designed to be more capable than its predecessor. Foundation says the robot has weather-resistant joints and modular parts that can be replaced in the field, along with a battery that can run for up to six hours, though heavier payloads reduce that figure. At maximum capacity, Pathak says the machine can walk while carrying 200 pounds, compared with roughly 50 to 60 pounds for the previous version.

The Phantom MKII can do so thanks to significant redesigns of its actuators, the motors and gearing that make its limbs move. Its joints have been shrunk to around three-quarters the size of its predecessor’s, Pathak says, while delivering more than 1.5 times the performance. Smaller also means somewhat cheaper. Pathak claims the company has halved its bill of materials cost while simplifying assembly to make large-scale manufacturing more practical.

The goal is to begin producing MKII robots in early 2027. Initially, the company hopes to manufacture several hundred before ramping up to a few thousand by the end of the year. Production will initially remain in the San Francisco Bay Area; Pathak claims most components now come from the U.S. or allied countries.

Alongside the hardware improvements, Foundation claims a significant leap forward in the software powering the machine. Its Cortex II artificial intelligence system is designed to learn physical tasks by observing humans perform them—requiring as few as 60 demonstrations for some tasks.

Pathak’s ambitions extend beyond construction sites and battlefields, though he rules out selling to countries that aren’t allied with the United States. In a manifesto published alongside the robot’s launch, Pathak outlines a vision of the future in which fleets of robots work in mining, materials processing, and construction. Humanoids could help bring the cost of a $1 million home down to between $60,000 and $80,000, he figures.

Beyond building your next home, the Phantom MKII could help keep it safe, too. Pathak is open to his robots taking on policing roles, provided they are deployed in ways that make people feel protected rather than intimidated. “I don’t think you can build a utopia and then not defend it,” he says.

#10320. It’s launch day for ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’. The 13-year wait is over at midnight

After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here.

“Grand Theft Auto VI” launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon.

The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X’S, meaning players in Asia and other regions will begin entering the game hours before its U.S. release.

New Zealand will be among the first countries where players can access the game and internet providers there are preparing for a surge in downloads as midnight arrives.

“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”

The company expects about 35 petabytes of additional traffic across its network, which Rodgers called “enormous.”

The expectations are enormous, too.

The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide, while “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.

Rockstar is returning to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following a game that became one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.

Game returns to Vice City after 13 years

At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.

Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.

Their relationship marks one of the biggest departures from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.

Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, stretching beyond Vice City into beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.

Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities. They flew over the Everglades and researched the area’s history and architecture.

Miami embraces its fictional alter ego

Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity.

Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release.

The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.

Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight.

In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack.

Years of hype arrive at launch day

Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.

The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.

The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.

“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.

The long wait is partly a product of the extraordinary staying power of its predecessor. “Grand Theft Auto Online,” the multiplayer component of “GTA V,” has kept players engaged for years through updates, activities and in-game purchases.

Music has long been woven into the “Grand Theft Auto” experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.

For “GTA VI,” Rockstar commissioned an original adaptive score from Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice. The music is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing. A 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.

What players will find next

Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.

The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.

Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.

Those answers will begin emerging first from players in Asia and Europe as midnight arrives in their regions, followed by North America hours later.

Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay and Tong-hyung Kim contributed to this report.

—Jonathan Landrum Jr., AP Entertainment Writer

#10319. What Breaks When a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Hits 1,000 Concurrent Streams

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

We sent 1,000 streaming calls at the same moment through three self-hosted LLM gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each gateway was limited to 2 CPUs. As shipped, Langfuse finished 261 of the 1,000 streams and LiteLLM finished 403. Neither failure came from the gateway's own code.

Langfuse's failures came from Linux's open-file limit, which Docker sets to 1,024 by default. LiteLLM had that problem too, plus a second one: an empty key cache sent hundreds of database lookups at once, and the ones that waited longer than 10 seconds were rejected. This article shows how each failure looked, how we traced it to its cause, and the settings that fixed it.

This benchmark measured the resource consumption of three LLM gateways under scaling concurrent streaming loads.

Full latency, memory, and feature results are available in the Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore benchmark.

First-token times are medians of the streams that succeeded. Up to 250 streams, every gateway succeeded. Then the errors started, and they did not look alike:

A 502 and a 503 point at different layers, so we expected two different causes. Two of the three turned out to share one cause.

Linux counts every network connection as an open file, and it caps how many open files one process may hold. The cap has two values. The soft limit is the cap that is in force now. The hard limit is the ceiling: a process may raise its own soft limit up to that value, and no further.

A streaming gateway holds two connections for each stream: one from the client, and one to the model provider. That makes about 1,000 open files at 500 streams, and about 2,000 at 1,000 streams. A gateway also needs a few more files for its database, its logs and its own libraries.

Docker on our machine gave every container a soft limit of 1,024 and a hard limit of 524,288. All three gateways received the same two numbers. What differed was how each program treats them when it starts:

Node.js raises its own soft limit to the hard limit at startup. The Rust and Python services keep 1,024, and neither project's Compose file sets a higher value. So the two gateways ran out of open files near 500 streams, which is the point where the errors started.

The out-of-files error appeared as a failed connection, not as a clear message. The Langfuse gateway's logs showed failed connections to OpenAI, and also failed connections to Langfuse's own web service, which the gateway asks to check each key. Both come from one cause: a process that cannot open another file cannot open another socket. Its client then receives a 502.

Read the limit the process actually has, not the one you think Docker gave it. Process 1 is usually the main process in a container:

If the gateway runs under a supervisor or several workers, check each worker's process ID instead of process 1. To see how close a process is to its limit under load, count its open file descriptors:

Raise the limit for the gateway service in its Compose file. We used 65,536 for all three gateways:

The same ulimits block works on the LiteLLM service. On Kubernetes or another platform, check /proc//limits inside a running container rather than assuming a value.

With the open-file limit raised, the Langfuse gateway finished all 1,000 streams. LiteLLM still returned 503 errors. To separate the two causes, we ran LiteLLM with one worker and only the open-file limit raised. All 500 streams succeeded in that ladder, but 595 of 1,000 failed with 503.

The 503 message names the authentication database, so we read LiteLLM's logs and its source. The log gave the same reason for all 840 failed streams in these runs, 595 in that ladder and 245 in the cold-cache runs below:

When 500 calls arrive while the key is not in the cache, each call looks the key up in Postgres. All of those lookups queue for 10 connections. The worker was also using its whole CPU allowance at this point, which slows every query it sends and receives. We infer that this CPU load lengthens the queue, but we did not measure it separately. Whatever the share of each, the lookups at the back of the queue miss the 10-second deadline.

If that explanation is right, the failures should depend on whether the key is already in the cache. So we ran 500 streams four more times. Three runs started after 75 seconds with no calls, which is longer than the 60-second cache. One run started right after a single warm-up call:

The warm run had no failures. The cold runs failed by different amounts, 161, 84 and 0, because the result depends on how many lookups miss the deadline, and that changes from run to run. This probably explains why the earlier ladder succeeded at 500 and failed at 1,000. A run is a race between the lookup queue and the deadline, so a single ladder does not show where the limit is.

The warm-up result is the one we measured. Send one call with each virtual key after LiteLLM starts, and avoid quiet periods longer than 60 seconds before a traffic spike. A steady flow of traffic keeps the key in the cache.

LiteLLM also exposes three settings that act on this path. We did not test them, so treat them as places to look rather than proven fixes:

We raised the open-file limit to 65,536 for all three gateways and gave LiteLLM 2 workers, one per CPU, as its production guide recommends for a single machine. Then we ran the full ladder again:

The open-file errors were gone for every gateway, and the Langfuse gateway gave the fastest first token of the three. LiteLLM still returned 120 × 503 at 500. That level started about 60 seconds after the first call of the ladder, so the cached key had probably just expired. All 1,000 succeeded at the next level, which started within 60 seconds of the 500 level.

Once nothing failed, CPU decided the first-token times. LiteLLM used its whole 2-CPU allowance from 100 streams on, and its median first token took 19.2 seconds at 1,000 streams. AcruxCore also used both CPUs from 100 streams on, and its first token at 1,000 streams was 3.8 s at the median and 9.7 s at p95. The Langfuse gateway peaked at 1.65 CPUs and 168 MiB, with a first token of 1.7 s at the median and 9.6 s at p95.

Each gateway also needs the rest of its stack, and that stack uses CPU too. While the Langfuse gateway served 500 streams, its whole stack used up to 3.1 CPUs, because the web service checked keys and the worker and ClickHouse stored usage. AcruxCore's whole stack peaked at 4.0 CPUs, because its API writes a trace for every call to Postgres. Size the stack around the gateway, not only the gateway container.

Talha Anwar is a senior AI and full-stack engineer and writes about building and running AI systems at talhaanwar.com.

#10318. Google Home update fixes Nest ‘Live View’ issues, improves Nest Hub and Gemini for speakers

A new Google Home update is rolling out with a fix for “Live View” issues affecting Nest Cam devices, improvements for the Nest Hub, upgrades for Gemini, and more.

As per usual, the latest Google Home update can be split up into a few categories, starting with Gemini. Still in early access, enrolled users can expect further improvements to smart home controls, faster timers, and “more conversational voice feedback,” as well as faster Broadcasts.

Most notable on the Gemini front is improvements to Nest Hubs, with smart displays now showing “relevant images when helpful” when you ask questions.

Visual answers with images on smart displays: On-screen answers on smart displays now will include relevant images when helpful so you can take in information at a glance.

In the Google Home app, Google is adding a “Google Home Premium” page to the settings menu, an “Eco Mode Everywhere” toggle for homes with multiple Nest Thermostats, and support for Home keys in Google Wallet for compatible locks.

More software updates are rolling out for older Nest Cam devices, including a fix for the “Live View” issue that’s been in place on some devices such as Nest Hello. You can also remove an unmigrated Nest Hello from the Home app even if it is offline. Other camera updates in this update include:

On the AI agent front, Google Home MCP connections now allow agents to control automations as well as accessing new controls and status checks across “thermostats, fans, air purifiers, robot vacuums, lighting effects, kitchen appliances, EV chargers, and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.”

Google is also rolling out smart speaker updates right now, but details on what’s new are limited.

#10317. Diffusers welcomes FLUX-2

FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series. It is an entirely new model with a new architecture and pre-training done from scratch! In this post, we discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2, performing inference with it under various setups, and LoRA fine-tuning.

🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a new image generation and editing model.

FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation. Furthermore, it can take multiple images as reference inputs, while producing the final output image. Below, we briefly discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2.

First, instead of two text encoders as in Flux.1, it uses a single text encoder — Mistral Small 3.1. Using a single text encoder greatly simplifies the process of computing prompt embeddings. The pipeline allows for a max_sequence_length of 512. Instead of using a single-layer output for the prompt embedding, FLUX.2 stacks outputs from intermediate layers, which have been known to be more beneficial.

FLUX.2 follows the same general multimodel diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) + parallel DiT architecture as Flux.1. As a refresher, MM-DiT blocks first process the image latents and conditioning text in separate streams, only joining the two together for the attention operation, and are thus referred to as “double-stream” blocks. The parallel blocks then operate on the concatenated image and text streams and can be regarded as “single-stream” blocks.

The key DiT changes from Flux.1 to FLUX.2 are as follows:

Time and guidance information (in the form of AdaLayerNorm-Zero modulation parameters) is shared across all double-stream and single-stream transformer blocks, respectively, rather than having individual modulation parameters for each block as in Flux.1.

None of the layers in the model use bias parameters. In particular, neither the attention nor feedforward (FF) sub-blocks of either transformer block use bias parameters in any of their layers.

In Flux.1, the single-stream transformer blocks fused the attention output projection with the FF output projection. FLUX.2 single-stream blocks also fuse the attention QKV projections with the FF input projection, creating a fully parallel transformer block:

Note that compared to the ViT-22B block depicted above, FLUX.2 uses a SwiGLU-style MLP activation rather than a GELU activation (and also doesn’t use bias parameters).

A larger proportion of the transformer blocks in FLUX.2 are single-stream blocks (8 double-stream blocks to 48 single-stream blocks, compared to 19/38 for Flux.1). This also means that single-stream blocks make up a larger proportion of the DiT parameters: Flux.1[dev]-12B has ~54% of its total parameters in the double-stream blocks, whereas FLUX.2[dev]-32B has ~24% of its parameters in the double-stream blocks (and ~73% in the single-stream blocks).

FLUX.2 uses a larger DiT and Mistral3 Small as its text encoder. When used together without any kind of offloading, the inference takes more than 80GB VRAM. In the following sections, we show how to perform inference with FLUX.2 in more accessible ways, under various system-level constraints.

Before you try out the following code snippets, make sure you have installed diffusers from main and have run hf auth login.

The above code snippet was tested on an H100, and it isn’t sufficient to run inference on it without CPU offloading. With CPU offloading enabled, this setup takes ~62GB to run.

Users who have access to Hopper-series GPUs can take advantage of Flash Attention 3 to speed up inference:

You can check out the supported attention backends (we have many!) here.

Using bitsandbytes, we can load the transformer and text encoder models in 4-bit, allowing owners of 24GB GPUs to use the model locally. You can run this snippet on a GPU with ~20 GB of free VRAM.

Notice that we're using a repository that contains the NF4-quantized versions of the FLUX.2 DiT and the Mistral text encoder.

Due to the modular design of a Diffusers pipeline, we can isolate modules and work with them in sequence. We decouple the text encoder and deploy it to an Inference Endpoint. This helps us with freeing up the VRAM usage for the DiT and VAE only.

⚠️ To use the remote text encoder, you need to have a valid token. If you are already authenticated, no further action is needed.

The example below uses a combination of local and remote inference. Additionally, we quantize the DiT with NF4 quantization through bitsandbytes.

You can run this snippet on a GPU with 18 GB of VRAM:

For GPUs with even lower VRAM, we have group_offloading, which allows GPUs with as little as 8GB of free VRAM to use this model. However, you'll need 32GB of free RAM. Alternatively, if you're willing to sacrifice some speed, you can set low_cpu_mem_usage=True to reduce the RAM requirement to just 10GB.

You can check out other supported quantization backends here and other memory-saving techniques here.

To check how different quantizations affect an image, you can play with the playground below or access it as standlone in the FLUX.2 Quantization experiments Space

FLUX.2 supports using multiple images as inputs, allowing you to use up to 10 images. However, keep in mind that each additional image will require more VRAM. You can reference the images by index (e.g., image 1, image 2) or by natural language (e.g., the kangaroo, the turtle). For optimal results, the best approach is to use a combination of both methods.

FLUX.2 supports advanced prompting techniques like structured JSON prompting, precise hex color control, and multi-reference image editing. Aside for the added control, this also allows for flexibility in changing specific attributes while maintaining others overall the same.For example, let's start with this json as the base schema (taken from the official FLUX.2 prompting guide):

Building up on that, let's turn it into a prompt for a shot of a good old fashion walkman on a carpet (simply pass this prompt to your chosen diffusers inference example from above):

Now, let's change the color of the carpet to a specific teal-blue shade (#367588) and add wired headphones plugged into the walkman:

The carpet color now matches the hex code provided, and the headphones have been with small changes to the overall scene.

Check out the official prompting guide for more examples and details.

Being both a text-to-image and an image-to-image model, FLUX.2 makes the perfect fine-tuning candidate for many use-cases! However, as inference alone takes more than 80GB of VRAM, LoRA fine-tuning is even more challenging to run on consumer GPUs. To squeeze in as much memory saving as we can, we utilize some of the inference optimizations described above for training as well, together with shared memory saving techniques, to substantially reduce memory consumption. To train it, you can use either the diffusers code below or Ostris' AI Toolkit.

We provide both text-to-image and image-to-image training scripts, for the purpose of this blog will focus on a text-to-image training example.

Many of these techniques complement each other and can be used together to reduce memory consumption further. However, some techniques may be mutually exclusive, so be sure to check before launching a training run.

Please make sure to check out the README for prerequisites before starting training.

The left image was generated using the pre-trained FLUX.2 model, and the right image was produced the LoRA.

#10316. How a tiny Italian soccer team plans to beat the biggest clubs in Europe

Como 1907 is a tiny European soccer team. It plays in a town of 85,000 people on Lake Como in northern Italy, where some Hollywood royalty live for part of the year. Its stadium holds only 12,000, which makes it a school playground next to Real Madrid’s 83,000-capacity Santiago Bernabéu. The owners of Como, Indonesia’s billionaire Hartono family, aim to beat Real Madrid, along with the likes of Paris Saint-Germain, Arsenal, and Bayern Munich.

Not on the pitch, necessarily, even though this year Como made it for the first time to the UEFA Champions League, the top club competition in Europe and the world. Its president, Mirwan Suwarso, wants to turn the little team into a financial powerhouse. Since Como will never match the TV and ticket money of Europe’s giants, he is trying to outgrow them as a brand. He wants Como to play in Disney’s league, not only the Champions League.

Suwarso sees soccer as the attraction. “There is a merchandise arm, the same as Disney,” he told The Observer in October. “The stadium, coming to a game, is the theme park. It is where you can touch and feel it, where you can experience the magic of Como.”

He expects nonsoccer revenue to overtake soccer revenue within two or three years, and already values the club at $1.1 billion. Como already has a fashion and hospitality business. You may have seen A-listers in its stands on Instagram. It sells match-day hospitality in rented lakeside villas, and its sister companies run a travel agency, a property arm, a youth academy, and a digital-content unit. Eventually, the club will offer more than that, as the brand’s presence expands across the world.

Como’s latest money-making move is kits. Adidas, current maker of its game jerseys and shorts, pays no sponsorship fee to Como, unlike some of the top teams in the world. European teams like Real Madrid get about $139 million a year on average. In addition to that, Real Madrid gets a 22.5% cut on anything with its brand sold through Adidas channels once sales pass a set threshold, along with bonuses for winning major titles like the Champions League or the Spanish league, La Liga. Como, like most teams, gets none of that.

Instead, Como and its small team brethren get gear for their teams. For Como, that’s $300,000 to $400,000 worth of it, which probably costs $100,000 to make, says Suwarso. He points out that they need to buy millions of dollars in kits from Adidas to sell to fans. From those sales they get a cut. Suwarso thinks this type of deal is upside down for small clubs. Adidas declined to comment for this story.

Suwarso’s answer is to own the whole chain, from the shirt’s design to the shop shelf. And they want to share this design, manufacturing, and distribution business with other small clubs so they all can get more money.

Como’s Adidas deal ends after the 2026-27 season. The club won’t renew it, and it plans to launch its own kit brand in June. Suwarso doesn’t pretend Como will make Real Madrid money this way. Real Madrid will make more because “of course, they’re bigger,” he said.

Peter Rohlmann, a German sports-marketing consultant who runs PR Marketing, a firm in Rheine, thinks Como is overreaching. In-house jerseys have failed within a few years in the vast majority of cases, even at big clubs, he says. Fans resist little-known labels, clubs underestimate the costs, and production never reaches real volume, he points out in an email interview. Napoli, another Italian soccer club, is the only one that survived with its Armani-designed kits. “All others have failed,” Rohlmann told the Sports Business Journal back in August.

Lecce, another team that plays in Italy’s Serie A league, tried to launch its own homemade brand, M908, starting in 2018. M908’s sales were only around $2.3 million a year, according to News Tank Football. This July, the club announced that Adidas would take over starting with the 2026-27 season.

Como’s management believes they can fix this volume problem by selling to other clubs. The club will join forces with “a historic Italian label”—Como hasn’t identified it yet—to make its new kit brand, according to FashionNetwork, while it dresses clubs across Europe and South America. Its Rhude 4 Fans line, launched in April 2026, already makes collections for Tottenham Hotspur and Everton in England’s Premier League, and Los Angeles FC, in Major League Soccer. The Observer counts 24 clubs that Como helps with merchandise. The kits are for “fellow unwanteds and undesirables,” says Suwarso. The teams that Nike, Adidas, and Puma won’t pay.

Como will carry the bill, says Alexandra Bell, the club’s chief communications officer. “We will underwrite production, marketing, and distribution costs, making it a no-risk proposition for partner clubs,” she tells Fast Company in an email. The kit’s design will be the product of “a collaboration between our creative team and our partner’s designers,” she says.

Bell tells me that only Como’s players will wear the new kits next season, as the company fine-tunes the manufacturing. “On the lifestyle side, this newly formed brand have already reached agreements to support nine other clubs next season, and that number continues to grow,” she says.

Como has its work cut out for it, as brands like Skechers, On (which got the French star Kylian Mbappé to promote its gear), New Balance, and Under Armour all try to gain a foothold in European soccer. Still, Bell is confident, given Como’s background in design and production.

“Just like any business, risk cannot be eliminated,” she tells me, but the club’s retail team already handles everything “from design, production and supply chain to logistics, distribution and e-commerce,” including six shops in Como itself and 585 affiliate shops across the province. In four years, she says, that operation grew from about $59,000 a year to a business that’s targeting about $44 million in annual revenue in 2026.

Perhaps Como will succeed where others failed. The club has a special allure, a je ne sais quoi that makes it very attractive to people. Part of it lies in its David-versus-Goliath story. The Hartonos helped the club mount a formidable comeback, taking the team back to Italy’s top division. (The club had been as low as the fourth tier of the Italian game at one point.) They surprised everyone last year, when Como finished fourth in Serie A. This got the club into the 2026-2027 Champions League, where it is near the top of the standings as of November. 

Another part of the club’s attraction is the high-class setting of Lake Como and all the glamour the stars who vacation there bring to the public’s collective imagination. Hugh Grant, Keira Knightley, Michael Fassbender, and Florence Pugh have all turned up at the Stadio Sinigaglia at one point. Many came while vacationing on the lake. The French soccer icon Thierry Henry and Como’s coach, Cesc Fàbregas—a FIFA World Cup winner with Spain—own stakes in the club. According to Goal, a former employee told La Gazzetta dello Sport, Italy’s leading sports daily, that the club treats famous guests to all-inclusive weekends. This helps Como position itself as an aspirational brand. 

Selling the experience

The Hartono brothers, Robert Budi and Michael, bought Como in 2019. Back then, the team was stuck in Italy’s fourth division, playing semi-professional soccer. It seemed like a losing team, but the brothers saw opportunity: a potentially huge business that could go well beyond the sport. Fashion, travel, hospitality, all built around the club and the picture-perfect Lake Como brand. 

The Hartonos set up Sent Retail, a sister company that shares a holding with a property arm and a travel agency. According to Gazzetta, the company is separate from the club. It also has its own retail and fashion arm. Called Curva, it sells its own label alongside other clubs’ merchandise. AC Milan gear is its best seller, Suwarso says. Curva also stocks Venezia, Bologna, and AS Roma gear, and more clubs are coming, Bell tells me.

“Our vision is for Curva to become a multibrand fashion destination inspired by football culture—think Kith for football culture,” she says, referring to the New York streetwear store.

They got Rhuigi Villaseñor—founder of the Los Angeles label Rhude and a Como shareholder—as its chief brand officer. He has been busy ever since. Villaseñor’s streetwear label Rhude worked with Adidas to drop limited-edition fourth kits. The club also worked with the Indonesian couture designer Didit Hediprasetyo to create the club’s main home and away jerseys, incorporating Lake Como water and marble patterns painted by the Switzerland-based artist Golnaz Jebelli.

The company got the Italian luxury menswear house Brioni to design the suits for the squad and the Milanese luggage maker Bric to make cobranded leather duffel bags and travel accessories. Hublot, the Swiss watchmaker, created a 50-piece limited-edition Classic Fusion black ceramic chronograph featuring the club crest.

The company also produces its own resortwear and leisure apparel via the Official Como 1907 Store under fictional country club labels like Como Sailing Club, Como Running Club, and Como Padel Club. There are Lago di Como lines for running, tennis, padel, and the outdoors. To give you an idea of price, they sell a quilted leather bomber for about $1,740.

Is it working?

That postcard travels well in every sense of the word. Only 38% of its merchandise is soccer gear, according to the Sunday Times. More than 40% of lifestyle sales come from the United States, versus around 17% from Italy, Suwarso said at the Pambianco-PwC Fashion Summit in Milan on November 11, according to FashionNetwork. Como is hunting for a flagship store in London, and Paris and Milan are next, Bell says.

According to Suwarso, more than 80% of the group’s nearly 300 employees don’t work in the club itself at all. The club, however, is still the key to it all. Its social following grew 202% in a year, to nearly 4 million. Stadium revenue nearly tripled in a year, from about $5.5 million to $15.5 million. Almost all of that jump came from hospitality, Suwarso told Business of Sport. While Como fans pay $23 for basic tickets, top hospitality packages reach about $2,900. “With a 12,000-seat stadium, there are limits to how much we can grow through match day revenue alone,” Bell says.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Destination Calcio (@destination.calcio)

For all of Suwarso’s optimism, Rohlmann sees a new Borussia Dortmund. The German club went public on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange in 2000, and Rohlmann says Como, like Dortmund back then, is trying things “out of euphoria and because of the need for storytelling.” Dortmund spent its IPO money on an expensive squad and a bigger stadium, sold the stadium and leased it back, and by 2005 was hours away from bankruptcy, with debts of around $140 million.

So far, however, the numbers seem to be on Suwarso’s side.

These aren’t audited figures but, in addition to the $44 million in annual retail revenue this year, the club itself claims its revenue also jumped from $11.4 million in the 2023-24 season to $64.3 million in 2024-25. But so did the losses: $122 million for the club itself in 2024-25 and $153 million for the whole group, according to Gazzetta.

Costs nearly tripled that season, to $184 million, with staff costs alone at $99 million, according to Calcio e Finanza, an Italian sports finance site. The Hartonos have put in about $450 million, much of it on players: Como has spent about $470 million on transfers since the 2023-24 season, according to Outside Sports, a sports business site. In June, Gazzetta predicted that Como would “inevitably exceed” the financial rules of UEFA, the European federation. These rules ban clubs from spending too much money beyond a certain level of financial loss. 

These rules are designed to avoid billionaires from using their resources to win competitions, even if their teams are losing money, thus making other clubs with no financial backup less competitive. “If you have to fine us, fine us,” Suwarso told Business of Sport. The club is expected to agree a settlement with UEFA around April or May 2027, according to Outside Sports.

Suwarso promises that the club will break even by the end of next season. “Our priority is a sustainable club,” Bell says. “Performance on the pitch is unpredictable, and commercial growth does not automatically translate into results.”

We will see soon enough. If Suwarso is right, Como will continue making more money selling its brand than playing with its crest. If Rohlmann is right, they will end up with the most expensive gift shop south of the Alps.
