#10279. 5 Best AI Anime Video Generators in 2026, and Are AI Anime Videos Worth Making?

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI video generators can now turn a prompt or a character image into a few seconds of animation, and anime is one of the most popular styles people ask for. But anime is also one of the hardest styles to get right: flat colors, thin linework and stylized motion expose the weaknesses of video models quickly. For developers and designers, the useful question is not which tool is “best”, but what each one actually offers, what it cannot do yet, and how to fit it into a real production workflow.

This article compares five generators on what their own pages state, covers the problems they all share, asks whether AI anime videos are worth making, and then explains how the models work and how designers and developers can build a practical workflow, including ffmpeg and API-integration examples. “Best” here depends on the job: the tools are listed in no ranking order, each is linked once to its official site for reference, and the comparison is based on public vendor pages reviewed in November 2026. Features, models and pricing change often, so verify current details before relying on any of them.

We reviewed each vendor’s own site and compared what it states on the same points. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a lab benchmark. Where a page does not state something, we say so instead of guessing.

AI anime video generator by Pollo AI sits within a general AI video platform. On its main site, Pollo describes generating video from text prompts or uploaded images and editing existing videos, such as adding, changing, removing or restyling content. It also offers AI image generation, so a character image and the animation can be made in one place.

Strengths for anime work: text-to-video and image-to-video in the same tool, plus video editing and restyling, which suits experimenting with looks.

Limitations and gaps: the pages we could read do not name the underlying models, list credit amounts or pricing, or describe anime-specific controls such as reference characters or first and last frame inputs. You will need to test consistency yourself.

Fits: creators who want image, video and editing tools in one platform and are comfortable testing results before committing.

Vidu lists text-to-video, image-to-video and reference-to-video modes. For image-to-video you can set first and last frames. Reference-to-video lets you upload several images of a character, object or scene, and saved references can be reused through a My References feature. The site highlights 2D animation and diverse artistic styles, mentions 1080p output and offers an API platform aimed at enterprise use.

Strengths for anime work: the clearest set of consistency tools among the five pages we reviewed, with first and last frames, multi-image references and reusable saved characters.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not specify clip durations beyond examples, detail its anime-specific templates, or list prices. Free credits are mentioned without an amount.

Fits: sequences built around a recurring character, and teams that want an API.

Kling AI presents Kling 4.0 for video, described as offering stable dynamic motion and an audio-visual experience, alongside an image model, a Motion Control tool and a node-based Canvas editor for working through scripts, storyboards, images and video. It also lists MCP and CLI support for batch generation and automated production, and an API platform with documentation.

Strengths for anime work: motion-focused tooling and a workflow environment for storyboards and multi-step production, plus automation options for developers.

Limitations and gaps: the page we reviewed does not detail image-to-video specifics, first and last frame controls, camera control, durations, video resolution or pricing, and it gives no anime-specific guidance.

Fits: teams that value motion control and scripted or batch pipelines.

Hailuo AI, from MiniMax, describes creating AI videos and images from text or photos. Its page shows a reference field and an Omni Reference option, a banner for a model that mentions multimodal generation and editing, and many photo-based templates such as photo-to-motion, transformation and style transfer.

Strengths for anime work: an accessible, template-driven way to animate a still image and try stylized effects quickly.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not explain how reference works, or state camera control, durations, resolution, API availability or pricing. Template-driven results may be harder to control precisely than prompt- and frame-driven workflows.

Fits: quick experiments and social clips made from a single image.

Dreamina describes itself as an all-in-one creative platform for images, videos and talking avatars. For video it lists text-to-video, image-to-video, sketch-to-video, cartoon video generation and reference-to-video, using several Seedance models, along with editing examples such as green-screen replacement. It also offers image generation and upscaling.

Strengths for anime work: a broad toolset, including cartoon-oriented generation, references and editing in one environment.

Limitations and gaps: no official maximum duration or video resolution is stated, and the page notes that displayed pricing is for reference only and that final pricing requires signing in. The breadth of features and models can make it harder to know which one to use for a given shot.

Fits: creators who want images, video and avatars under one roof.

“Not stated” means the vendor page we reviewed did not say, not that the feature does not exist. Treat the table as a checklist of questions to answer in your own tests.

It depends on the job and on what you compare them with. Against a full studio production they are limited. Against having no animation at all, they change what a small team or solo creator can attempt.

Treat the generator as a fast prototyping and shot-making assistant, not a replacement for writing, direction and design. Audience reaction also varies, and some viewers are openly critical of AI-made work, so quality and disclosure both matter.

Most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

Create an original character sheet with front, side and three-quarter views, a fixed color palette and a clear silhouette. Keep it simple: fewer fine details means less flicker.

Break the sequence into short shots with one action and one camera move each. A four-shot, twenty-second sequence is more realistic than one long generation.

Start each shot from a clean keyframe of your character. Where a tool supports first and last frames or reference images, use them to define the pose and keep identity stable.

Describe subject, action, camera and mood, and add a style anchor. For example: “The girl slowly turns toward the camera, wind moves her hair, petals drift past, gentle push-in, 2D cel shading, clean linework.”

Scrub through each clip for warped hands, drifting faces and flickering lines. Discard or regenerate failures instead of hoping nobody notices.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

Developers can make the pipeline repeatable. Two patterns help: scripted post-processing with ffmpeg, and a resilient job-based client for any generation API.

The script below extracts a last frame to seed the next shot, normalizes clips to a common size and frame rate so they can be joined, concatenates them, and optionally holds each frame twice for an “on twos” look. Adjust sizes and frame rates to your project.

Video generation is usually asynchronous: you submit a job, then poll or receive a callback. The sketch below shows the pattern with a timeout and backoff. The endpoints and fields are placeholders, so follow your provider’s documentation for real ones.

Most are diffusion models for video. They start from noise and remove it step by step across a sequence of frames, guided by a text prompt and often a starting image or reference images, until coherent motion appears.

Usually, for consistency. The image locks the character and style, while the prompt only needs to describe motion.

Thin lines and flat color regions make small frame-to-frame changes visible. Simpler designs, slower motion and post-processing reduce it.

Partly. Reference images, saved characters and shared keyframes help, but you should still review every shot for drift.

For short clips, concept previews and storyboards, often yes. For long, dialogue-driven stories, not yet.

It depends on the tool and plan. Read the current terms and make sure you have rights to any characters or assets you upload.

Run the same character image and prompt through each, then compare consistency, line stability, motion quality and cost per usable second.

AI anime video generators are useful, but uneven. The five tools reviewed here differ in input modes, consistency tools, developer access and how much their own pages say, and none removes the core problems of consistency, flicker and limited acting. The practical approach is to test several tools on the same shots, keep your workflow tool-agnostic, design characters that are simple and consistent, and review every clip before it ships. Used that way, they are a capable prototyping and shot-making aid, not a substitute for design and direction.

#10278. Tokenization in Transformers v5: Simpler, Clearer, and More Modular

Transformers v5 redesigns how tokenizers work. The big tokenizers reformat separates tokenizer design from trained vocabulary (much like how PyTorch separates neural network architecture from learned weights). The result is tokenizers you can inspect, customize, and train from scratch with far less friction.

TL;DR: This blog explains how tokenization works in Transformers and why v5 is a major redesign, with clearer internals, a clean class hierarchy, and a single fast backend. It’s a practical guide for anyone who wants to understand, customize, or train model-specific tokenizers instead of treating them as black boxes.

For experts: If you're already familiar with the concepts and want to understand the changes in v5, go to v5 Separates Tokenizer Architecture from Trained Vocab

Before diving into the changes, let's quickly cover what tokenization does and how the pieces fit together.

Language models don't read raw text. They consume sequences of integers usually called token IDs or input IDs. Tokenization is the process of converting raw text into these token IDs. (Try the tokenization playground here to visualize tokenization.)

Tokenization is a broad concept used across natural language processing and text processing generally. This post focuses specifically on tokenization for Large Language Models (LLMs) using the transformers and tokenizers libraries.

Ġworld (above) is a single token that represents the character sequence " world" (with the space).

A token is the smallest string unit the model sees. It can be a character, word, or subword chunk like "play" or "##ing" ("##" is a pattern, don't worry if you don't completely understand it now 🤗). The vocabulary maps each unique token to the token ID.

A good tokenizer compresses text into the smallest amount of tokens. Fewer tokens means more usable context without increasing model size. Training a tokenizer boils down to finding the best compression rules for your datasets. For example, if you work on Chinese corpus you can sometimes find very nice surprises 😉.

Tokenization happens in stages. Each stage transforms text before passing it to the next:

Each component is independent. You can swap normalizers or change the algorithm without rewriting everything else.

You can access the rust based tokenizer through _tokenizer. We go in more depth about it in this section

The following algorithms dominate modern language model tokenizers:

The tokenizers library is a Rust-based tokenization engine. It is fast, efficient, and completely language model agnostic. The library handles the mechanics of converting text into token IDs and back. The tokenizers library is a general-purpose tool that implements the tokenization algorithms, but does not implement the conventions that connect those algorithms to specific language models.

Consider what happens when you use tokenizers directly with the SmolLM3-3B model:

The output is raw tokenization. You get token IDs and the string pieces they correspond to. Nothing more.

Now consider what's missing. The SmolLM3-3B is a conversational model. When you interact with it, you typically structure your input as a conversation with roles like "user" and "assistant". The language model expects special formatting tokens to indicate these roles. The raw tokenizers library has no concept of any of this.

The transformers library bridges this gap. The library is primarily known as a model definition library, but it also provides a tokenizer abstraction layer that wraps the raw tokenizers backend and adds model-aware functionality.

Here's the same tokenization with the transformers wrapper:

Notice how the special tokens like <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> are applied to the prompt before tokenizing. This is useful for the model to learn where a new sequence starts and ends.

The transformers tokenizer adds everything the raw library lacks:

transformers implements the tokenization API that is most commonly used in the entire ML community (encode, decode, convert_tokens_to_ids, etc.)

The transformers library organizes tokenizers into a class hierarchy. At the top sits a base class that defines the common interface. Below it, backend classes handle the actual tokenization using different engines. At the bottom, model-specific classes configure the backends for particular models.

PreTrainedTokenizerBase is the abstract base class for all tokenizers in transformers. It defines the interface that every tokenizer must implement.

The base class handles functionality that doesn't depend on the tokenization backend:

Every tokenizer in transformers ultimately inherits from PreTrainedTokenizerBase. The base class ensures consistent behavior across all tokenizers, regardless of which backend they use for the actual tokenization.

TokenizersBackend is the primary backend class for most modern tokenizers. It inherits from PreTrainedTokenizerBase and wraps the Rust-based tokenizers library.

The class stores the Rust tokenizer object internally:

When you call encoding methods on a TokenizersBackend tokenizer, the class delegates the actual tokenization to the Rust backend:

The Rust backend performs computationally intensive work, while the Python wrapper adds the model-aware features on top.

Many model-specific tokenizers inherit from TokenizersBackend, examples include:

These model-specific classes configure the backend with the correct vocabulary, merge rules, special tokens, and normalization settings for their respective models.

PythonBackend inherits from PreTrainedTokenizerBase and implements tokenization in pure Python. The class is aliased as PreTrainedTokenizer.

The pure-Python backend exists for several reasons:

The Python backend is slower than the Rust backend. For most use cases, the Rust-backed TokenizersBackend is preferred.

Model-specific tokenizers that inherit from PythonBackend (or its alias PreTrainedTokenizer) include some older or specialized models, like:

SentencePieceBackend inherits from PythonBackend and provides integration with Google's SentencePiece library. SentencePiece is a standalone tokenization library that many models use, particularly those trained by Google.

The backend wraps a SentencePiece processor:

Models that use SentencePiece tokenization inherit from this backend. Examples include:

The SentencePiece backend inherits from PythonBackend rather than directly from PreTrainedTokenizerBase because it shares much of the same interface and padding/truncation logic.

AutoTokenizer is the recommended entry point for loading tokenizers. It automatically determines which tokenizer class to use for a given model and returns an instance of that class.

Behind the scenes, AutoTokenizer performs these steps:

The benefit of AutoTokenizer is that you don't need to know which tokenizer class a model uses. Whether a model uses LlamaTokenizer, GPT2Tokenizer, or BertTokenizer, the same AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("model-name") call works.

The tokenizer system in transformers forms a layered architecture:

The most significant change in Transformers v5 is a philosophical shift in how tokenizers are defined. Tokenizers now work like PyTorch's nn.Module: you define the architecture first, then fill it with learned parameters.

In v4, tokenizers were black boxes tied to pretrained checkpoint files. If you loaded LlamaTokenizerFast, you couldn't easily answer basic questions about it:

The __init__ method gave no clues. You had to dig through serialized files or external documentation to understand what the tokenizer actually did.

v4 also maintained two parallel implementations for every model:

Worst of all, you couldn't create an empty tokenizer architecture. If you wanted to train a LLaMA-style tokenizer on your own data, there was no clean way to instantiate a "blank" LLaMA tokenizer and fill it with your vocabulary and merges. Tokenizers existed only as loaded checkpoints, not as configurable templates.

v5 treats tokenizer architecture (normalizer, pre-tokenizer, model type, post-processor, decoder) as distinct from trained parameters (vocabulary, merges). This mirrors how PyTorch separates model architecture from learned weights.

The tokenizer class now explicitly declares its structure. Looking at LlamaTokenizer in v5, you can immediately see:

This transparency was impossible in v4, where the same information was buried in serialized files.

v5 consolidates the two-file system into a single file per model. LlamaTokenizer now inherits from TokenizersBackend, which wraps the Rust-based tokenizer that was previously exposed as the “fast” implementation and is now the default.

The former “slow” Python implementation lives explicitly behind PythonBackend, and SentencePieceBackend remains for models that require it, but Rust-backed tokenization is the preferred default.

Users now have one clear entry point. Advanced users who need to customize can still access lower-level components, but the library no longer forces everyone to navigate two parallel implementations.

Suppose you want a tokenizer that behaves exactly like LLaMA's – same normalization, same pre-tokenization, same BPE model type – but trained on a domain-specific corpus (medical text, legal documents, a new language). In v4, this required manually reconstructing the tokenizer pipeline from low-level tokenizers library primitives. In v5, you can instantiate the architecture directly and call train:

The resulting tokenizer will have your custom vocabulary and merge rules, but will process text identically to how a standard LLaMA tokenizer would with the same whitespace handling, same special token conventions, same decoding behavior.

The shift from "tokenizers as loaded checkpoints" to "tokenizers as configurable architectures" makes the library more modular, more transparent, and more aligned with how practitioners think about building ML systems.

Transformers v5 brings three improvements to tokenization:

The wrapper layer between tokenizers and Transformers remains essential. It adds model awareness, context lengths, chat templates, special tokens, that raw tokenization doesn't provide. V5 just makes that layer clearer and more customizable.

If you are looking to learn more about tokenization here are some resources:

Experiment with and compare different tokenizers

#10277. Pebblebee’s latest Android Find Hub trackers try some festive colors, but fall short on sparkle

Available now, Pebblebee’s latest Android Find Hub tracker color drop might also be the first real miss, with the festive theme falling short of what it’s supposed to look like.

Pebblebee has been dropping limited-time color variants of its Clip 5 tracker for Android Find Hub and Apple Find My all year, with the latest release this week including “Cranberry” and “Champagne.”

The new drop looks nice in marketing photos, but I will say, this is the first time I’ve felt the colors have missed the mark in person. “Cranberry” is a nice red color, but the bits of reflective sparkle shown in Pebblebee’s images don’t translate very well into real life. “Champagne” takes that a step further, with a very muted beige color that doesn’t have the shine seen in some of the listing photos.

They still look nice enough, just know you’re not getting the flashy, festive colors.

The good news, though, is that you’re still getting the same core hardware. USB-C rechargeable battery, support for Android Find Hub and Apple Find My, 130dB siren, and more, all for the usual $34.99.

The previous “Hotline Pink” and “Techno Lime” are still available for a limited time, and Pebblebee’s website has a Black Friday sale live, offering 20-30% off when you buy multiple trackers and use the code “BFCM26” at checkout.

Following reports that ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is plotting a return to the company, President Donald Trump has voiced his own support for such a move, Bloomberg reports. However, according to new insight from CNBC, Nvidia's board of directors is not considering the move and is instead focused on its ongoing investigation into Huang's extramarital affairs and a national security investigation, likely into possible allegations of chip smuggling into China.

Trump reportedly made his comments in support of Huang's return to reporters at the White House on Monday, ahead of his trip to Asia. "I would not mind that," he said. "A lot of people are asking Jensen; they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.” While Trump noted Huang's financial situation, he said the CEO did not put national security at risk and did not know Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

Last week, the President said that Apple's former CEO Tim Cook was the only man to replace Huang in Nvidia's top job. Trump's comments also contrast sharply with those of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who this week has called for Nvidia to replace Huang with an outsider, while giving the company 100 days to explain its dealings with China.

As mentioned, Jensen Huang's purported return does not seem to be an option the board is seriously considering. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the board of directors is focused on investigating Huang's conduct and a national security investigation and is not discussing his return.

A large petition has started circulating pertaining to Huang's reinstatement, with Elon Musk the most notable to sign. Musk had ventured so far as to say it would be an 'honor' to hire Huang, presumably to his Terafab project, following revelations of his exit.

While rumblings of possible illicit chip smuggling into China have dogged Nvidia for well over a year, Huang's tenure as founder and CEO ended somewhat abruptly last week after a series of revelations spiraled to bring about his resignation. In the wake of reports that US officials were said to be concerned about his close relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, it later transpired that Huang had indeed had an affair with Ms. Huang, and that there were suspicions she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Since that news broke, it has further been revealed that Huang also had an inappropriate relationship with one of his direct reports, Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell, and that the company covered up the fling. Perhaps more concerningly for Jensen Huang, it has been alleged that Ms. Huang and Megaspeed may have been involved in chip smuggling into China to the tune of more than $7 billion, with hundreds of thousands of H100 and H200 chips said to have found their way into the country at her behest, a factor analysts believe may be the true reason behind Huang's exit.

#10273. AprielGuard: A Guardrail for Safety and Adversarial Robustness in Modern LLM Systems

Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly evolved from text-only assistants into complex agentic systems capable of performing multi-step reasoning, calling external tools, retrieving memory, and executing code. With this evolution comes an increasingly sophisticated threat landscape: not only traditional content safety risks, but also multi-turn jailbreaks, prompt injections, memory hijacking, and tool manipulation.

In this work, we introduce AprielGuard, an 8B parameter safety–security safeguard model designed to detect:

AprielGuard is available in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, enabling explainable classification when needed and low-latency classification for production pipelines.

Traditional safety classifiers primarily focus on a limited classification spectrum (e.g., toxicity or self-harm), assume short inputs, and evaluate single user messages. Modern deployments, however, feature:

As a result, production teams increasingly rely on workarounds: multiple guard models for different stages, regex filters, static rules, or hand-crafted heuristics. These approaches are brittle and do not scale.

AprielGuard addresses these issues with a unified model and a unified safety + adversarial taxonomy, built specifically for modern LLM agent ecosystems.

AprielGuard operates across three input formats:

(These 16 categories are inspired from SALAD-Bench)

The model detects and evaluates a wide range of adversarial prompt patterns designed to manipulate model behavior or evade safety mechanisms. The model outputs a binary classification (e.g., adversarial / non_adversarial) rather than fine-grained attack categories.

The training data covers diverse adversarial types such as role-playing, world-building, persuasion, and stylization, among many other complex prompt manipulation strategies. These examples represent only a subset of the broader adversarial scenarios incorporated in the training data.

Synthetic data: AprielGuard is trained on a synthetically generated training dataset. The training data points are generated at a sub-topic level of the taxonomy for better coverage. We leverage Mixtral-8x7B and internally developed uncensored models to generate unsafe content for training purposes. Models were prompted with higher temperature to induce output variation. Prompting templates are meticulously tailored to ensure accurate data generation. Adversarial attacks are constructed using a combination of synthetic data points, diverse prompt templates, and rule-based generation techniques. We leveraged NVIDIA NeMo Curator to generate large-scale, multi-turn conversational datasets featuring complex, realistic scenarios with iterative and evolving attacks through context switches. This approach enabled us to systematically synthesize diverse interaction patterns, improving the robustness of the model to long-horizon reasoning, adversarial turns, and evolving user intent. We also used SyGra framework for synthetic data generation processes for harmful prompts and attacks generation. The training dataset encompasses diverse content formats such as conversational dialogues, forum posts, tweets, instructional prompts, questions, and how-to guides.

Data augmentation: To enhance model robustness, a range of data augmentation techniques were applied to the training data. These augmentations are designed to expose the model to natural variations and perturbations that commonly occur in real-world scenarios. Specifically, the dataset includes transformations such as character-level noise, insertion of typographical errors, leetspeak substitutions, word-level paraphrasing, and syntactic reordering. Such augmentations help the model generalize better by reducing sensitivity to superficial variations in input, thereby improving resilience against adversarial manipulations and non-standard text representations.

Agentic workflows: Agentic workflows represent real-world scenarios where autonomous agents execute multi-step tasks involving planning, reasoning, and interaction with tools, APIs, and other agents. These workflows often include sequences of user prompts, system messages, intermediate reasoning steps, and tool invocations, making them susceptible to diverse attack vectors. To construct these training data points, we synthetically generate a wide range of scenarios across multiple domains, capturing realistic agentic interactions between a user and an agentic system. Each data point is enriched with detailed contextual elements—including tool definitions, tool invocation logs, agent roles and policies, execution traces, conversation history, memory states, and scratch-pad reasoning. For malicious or adversarial examples, we corrupt the relevant segment of the workflow to reflect a specific attack vector. Depending on the scenario, this may involve modifying user prompts, altering intermediate reasoning traces, modifying the tool outputs, injecting false memory states, or disrupting inter-agent communication. By systematically perturbing different components of the agentic workflow, we produce high-fidelity examples that expose a model to a diverse spectrum of realistic and challenging attack patterns. Each data point was simulated to reflect realistic executions, incorporating both benign and adversarial sequences.

Long context use cases: We curated a specialized long context dataset composed of diverse, high-length use cases such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) work-flows, multi-turn conversational threads, incident details, and operational reports containing detailed communications. These examples simulate real-world environments where large text contexts are typical.

AprielGuard is built on top of an Apriel-1.5 Thinker Base variant, downscaled to an 8B configuration for efficient deployment.

AprielGuard performance on the public safety benchmarks.

A comparative assessment of model performance using aggregated results from safety benchmarks.

AprielGuard performance on the public adversarial benchmarks.

A comparative assessment of model performance using aggregated results from adversarial benchmarks.

We curated an internal benchmark dataset aimed at evaluating the detection of Safety Risks and Adversarial Attacks within agentic workflows. To construct this benchmark, we systematically designed multiple attack scenarios targeting different components of the workflow—such as prompt inputs, reasoning traces, tool parameters, memory states, and inter-agent communications. Each instance was annotated according to the taxonomy of vulnerabilities. Each workflow was simulated to reflect realistic executions, incorporating both benign and adversarial sequences. The dataset captures granular attack points across various stages such as planning, reasoning, execution, and response generation to provide fine-grained evaluation of model robustness. Overall, the dataset comprises a balanced mixture of safety risks and adversarial attacks.

Safety performance of different models on the agentic benchmark.

Adversarial performance of different models on the agentic benchmark..

Many real world safety or adversarial risks do not manifest in short, isolated text snippets, but rather emerge across use cases such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflows, multi-turn conversational threads, organizational incident details, and operational reports containing detailed communications. A guardian model must therefore detect subtle or "needle-in-a-haystack" cases, where malicious or manipulative content is sparsely distributed, embedded across multiple references, or intentionally obscured within benign text.

To evaluate AprielGuard’s long-context reasoning capabilities, we curated a specialized test dataset composed of diverse, high-length use cases. We considered the data upto 32k tokens for this evaluation. The baseline data was initially constructed from benign content representative of these domains. Malicious elements were then systematically injected to simulate adversarial or unsafe scenarios while maintaining the overall coherence of the text. For example, in an incident case summarization, an injection could be embedded within the case description, hidden in a metadata section, or inserted as part of a comment thread. Similarly, in multi-turn dialogue data, adversarial content might appear mid-conversation, near the end or at the beginning to test long range dependency tracking.

A major limitation in the current landscape of content moderation research is the scarcity of high- quality multilingual benchmarks. To address this gap and comprehensively assess the multilingual capabilities of AprielGuard, we extended the Safety Risks benchmarks and Adversarial Attack benchmarks into multiple non-English languages. The translation process was conducted using the MADLAD400-3B-MT model, a multilingual machine translation model based on the T5 architecture.

For this study, we selected eight of the most widely used non-English languages to ensure broad linguistic and geographical coverage: French, French-Canadian, German, Japanese, Dutch, Spanish, Portuguese-Brazilian, and Italian. Each instance from the English Safety and Adversarial benchmarks was translated into the eight target languages. During translation, we preserved the original English role identifiers, such as User: and Assistant:, while translating only the conversational content. This design choice ensures alignment with AprielGuard’s moderation framework, where the role context plays a crucial part in evaluating safety and adversarial intent.

As LLMs move toward deeply integrated agentic systems, the need for unified pipelines becomes more critical. AprielGuard is a step toward that future — reducing complexity, improving coverage, and offering a scalable foundation for trustworthy AI deployments.

Language Coverage: While AprielGuard has been primarily trained on English data, limited testing indicates it performs reasonably well across several languages, including: English, German, Spanish, French, French (Canada), Italian, Dutch, and Portuguese (Brazil). However, thorough testing and calibration are strongly recommended before deploying the model for production use in non-English settings.

Adversarial Robustness: Despite targeted training on adversarial and manipulative behaviors, the model may still exhibit vulnerability to complex or unseen attack strategies.

Domain Sensitivity: AprielGuard may underperform on highly specialized or technical domains (e.g., legal, medical, or scientific contexts) that require nuanced contextual understanding.

Latency–Interpretability Trade-off: Enabling reasoning traces enhances explainability but increases latency and compute cost. For low-latency or large-scale use cases, non-reasoning mode is recommended.

Reasoning Mode Sensitivity: The model exhibits occasional inconsistencies in classification outcomes between reasoning-enabled and non-reasoning inference modes.

Intended use: AprielGuard is intended strictly for use as a safeguard and risk assessment model. It classifies potential safety risks and adversarial threats according to the AprielGuard unified taxonomy. Any deviation from the prescribed inference may lead to unintended, unsafe, or unreliable behavior.

Rubin HPC puts "over 50,000" CUDA cores on a chip, implies four-die layout

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Supercomputing 2026 conference is under way, and despite continuing turmoil elsewhere in the company, Nvidia has lots to reveal at the show. Foremost among its announcements today, Nvidia took the wraps off a new member of the Rubin GPU family called Rubin HPC, a chip that the company says is meant to accelerate agentic workflows and simulation for scientists, engineers, and analysts working with large data sets.

To accelerate those most demanding workloads, Nvidia says Rubin HPC has the highest number of CUDA cores on any of its GPUs - "more than 50,000" - which might imply that this chip uses a configuration similar to the four-die Rubin Ultra GPU, which links those dies together using NVLink-C2C.

Today's Rubin GPU has 224 SMs and 28,672 CUDA cores, so scaling compute resources to the degree Rubin HPC does would necessarily require more dies on a package. Nvidia didn't reveal more details of the chip's physical layout alongside the announcement. (The representative image shared by the company wouldn't appear to take this into account.)

To keep data moving between Rubin HPC GPUs, Nvidia will use its NVLink 7 interconnect. The company didn't share any new details of the bandwidth or physical layer of this interconnect within the rack, but past disclosures about the tech have indicated that it retains the 3.6 TB/s of per-GPU bandwidth that NVLink 6 delivers while enlarging the size of its scale-up domain.

Nvidia didn't share any details of the Rubin HPC GPU's HBM capacity or bandwidth, and it also didn't share whether this part includes a rebalancing of compute resources towards native FP64, as AMD and Intel are touting at the conference with their own GPUs this week.

Nvidia instead touts the suitability of this chip for scientists and engineers using agentic workflows, for which the company expects faster simulation performance and therefore faster opportunities for discovery in those fields thanks to better agent performance in those domains.

In fields like climate research, genomic analysis, and financial simulation, Nvidia says the Rubin HPC GPU's "balanced design," with both higher compute resources and (presumably) faster data movement between nodes, will help feed the chip with the massive data sets typical of those workloads, minimizing idle compute resources and achieving better utilization.

Researchers, engineers, and analysts marshaling agent swarms to explore the problem spaces in their domains will also be able to take advantage of Nvidia's CUDA-X domain-specific libraries to boost performance on Rubin HPC, tightening the reasoning loop from hypothesis to simulation to refinement and hastening the pursuit of the most promising results.

Nvidia says Rubin HPC will arrive sometime in 2028.

#10270. This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Con, my family and I can’t stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2, we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo’s Zero 2 controllers for games that don’t use analog thumbsticks. I’ve spent years hunting for an alternative that pairs the size of the Zero 2 with as much of the functionality of a larger controller as I can get, and CRKD’s new Atom Plus is nearly exactly that. But if you have larger hands like I do, you may find the gamepad’s focus on portability a struggle.

Measuring around 3.5 inches wide, the $29.99 Atom Plus is about a half-inch smaller than the 8BitDo Zero 2 but squeezes in considerably more features and functionality. The most obvious is a pair of symmetrical analog thumbsticks with anti-drift tunneling magnetoresistance technology. You also get shoulder buttons and triggers, rumble feedback, a dedicated home button, motion controls, and customization through a mobile app.

Like many third-party controllers, the Atom Plus works with multiple platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2, PCs, Android, iOS, and various smart TVs. And just like other gamepads, pairing to different devices requires putting the Atom Plus into one of several Bluetooth modes by holding down a combination of buttons at power-up, which in this case is the home button plus a specific direction on the D-pad. It’s easy to do, but never easy to remember: I frequently needed to grab the manual or quickly Google which direction I need to press when switching devices. The Atom Plus already features a bunch of technical info etched into the back of the controller, so I’d love to see these important pairing instructions included there, too. (And that goes for all multiplatform gamepads.)

I primarily tested the Atom Plus with the Nintendo Switch 2 since I mostly plan to use the controller as a travel accessory. The thumbsticks are about the same size as those on the original Switch Joy-Con, which means they’re smaller than the Switch 2’s. And while I prefer an asymmetrical layout, the Atom Plus’ sticks are very good, with a little more tension than Nintendo’s that I find actually helps with precision movements given their limited travel.

While the overall build quality feels excellent, the Atom Plus’ tiny footprint creates some compromises and challenges. The front action buttons and D-pad feel nice and squishy, but the gamepad’s controls are a little crowded. When pressing down or right on the D-pad, my thumb regularly bumps the left thumbstick. It doesn’t hinder gameplay, but I do find it an annoying distraction.

The shoulder buttons use digital microswitches, as do the triggers, which means the latter can’t be used for racing games that support analog acceleration controls. I like that the two sets of buttons on the top edge sit at slightly different heights, but I would have preferred a little more differentiation since I’ve occasionally accidentally pressed the triggers when I meant to hit the shoulder buttons.

I was impressed with the Atom Plus’ customizability, however. When paired to an accompanying mobile app, you can check the controller’s remaining charge, turn off rumble feedback, see its unique product number (by tapping your phone to an NFC chip inside the controller), and remap any of its controls. That includes the pair of dual-function shortcut levers that replicate the Switch’s plus and minus buttons and screenshot shortcut.

Those levers move up and down and cleverly reduce the number of buttons crowding the front of the Atom Plus, but they feel a little too small, which is more or less the general theme. It’s a tiny gamepad that’s great for travel or stashing in your everyday carry. But, unsurprisingly, it probably won’t find its way into your regular gaming rotation. It’s assumed that players will be willing to settle for the compromise of occasionally contorting their fingers in weird, new ways for one of the smallest fully featured controllers on the market.

I don’t think a dual-stick controller could get any smaller than the Atom Plus without making too many ergonomic compromises. So while I applaud CRKD for the careful balancing act behind the Atom Plus’ design, and would certainly recommend it for those wanting a very capable controller that’s also cheap and portable, I’m now curious how it compares to Microsoft’s recently announced Xbox Nano controller that’s “surprisingly comfortable,” according to The Verge’s Tom Warren. It’s $20 more expensive than CRKD’s and noticeably larger, but it adds analog triggers, a more spacious design, and stubby grips making it easier to hold for those of us with beefy mitts.

#10269. Galaxy SmartTag 3 at $20 makes a compelling case to skip the Google Pixel Tag

Barely a week after its launch, Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is already on sale for as little as $20, making it a fairly compelling alternative to Google’s new Pixel Tag, assuming you have a Galaxy phone, of course.

While Google’s Pixel Tag is a brilliant launch, it’s not perfect. Still based on a Find Hub network that struggles to keep up, the Pixel Tag is a great choice for most Android users, but Galaxy devices have an alternate option.

Surprisingly, Samsung’s network often outperforms Google’s in real-life use, as many have found.

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 went on sale just a week ago as Samsung’s latest tracker. It’s still $29.99 and has a new, smaller design without a built-in mounting loop, but it brings upgrades in longer battery life, limited iPhone support, and a new NFC feature that can show your contact info if someone finds your lost tracker.

Woot is selling an international version of the Smarttrack 3. In addition to lacking Samsung's warranty it is unclear if the UWB functionality on these trackers will be compatible in the U.S.

Woot has the Galaxy SmartTag 3 for $23.99. That’s for a single tracker, but there are also discounted bundles. $43.99 for a 2-pack, $62.99 for a 3-pack, and $79.99 for a 4-pack. The 4-pack is the best deal per tracker at $20, but you’re saving money regardless of how many you pick up.

Meanwhile, Galaxy SmartTag 2 is also discounted at Amazon, should you prefer that hardware.

Lux is the first of two machines AMD is developing as part of a $1 billion deal with the DOE.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With the coming of SC26, also comes a fresh edition of the TOP500 list, which ranks the world's most powerful supercomputers. The newly released list illustrates that AMD powers 40% of the list, up 14% compared to 2025. AMD-powered systems now tally up to 202 on the list, up from 177 last year. New to the list is Lux, a “SI + HPC supercomputer” developed by AMD and the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), which debuted at position 14.

AMD’s representation in the top 10 is familiar. After debuting in June, China’s LineShine remains in the top slot. El Capitan, powered by AMD chips, is in the second slot, followed by Frontier in third, HPC7 in sixth, and HPC6 in eighth, the same as the most recent TOP500 list.

Lux was announced a little over a year ago in a $1 billion deal between the DOE and AMD to develop two supercomputers. This is the first of the two, and the first time it’s been on the TOP500. The system was built by HPE and developed by AMD and DOE as part of the U.S. government’s Genesis Mission. The machine is housed in Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF), alongside machines like Frontier.

Lux relies on over 4,000 Instinct MI355X GPUs separated into over 500 nodes. For HPC workloads using FP64, the machine is capable of 317 PetaFLOPS. For AI training, the machine peaks at 20 ExaFLOPS of FP8, and for inference, 40 ExaFLOPS of FP4. With 288 GB of HBM3E per GPU, the entire system has access to 1.1 PB.

The machine uses AMD EPYC host CPUs — we weren’t able to find details on the specific generation— and AMD’s Pensando networking, with nodes built inside HPE’s ProLiant Compute XD685.

LingKun, LX2 304C 1.55GHz, LingQi, Kylin OS

HPE Cray EX255a, AMD 4th Gen EPYC 24C 1.8GHz, AMD Instinct MI300A, Slingshot-11, TOSS

HPE Cray EX235a, AMD Optimized 3rd Generation EPYC 64C 2GHz, AMD Instinct MI250X, Slingshot-11, HPE Cray OS

HPE Cray EX - Intel Exascale Compute Blade, Xeon CPU Max 9470 52C 2.4GHz, Intel Data Center GPU Max, Slingshot-11

BullSequana XH3000, GH Superchip 72C 3GHz, NVIDIA GH200 Superchip, Quad-Rail NVIDIA InfiniBand NDR200, RedHat Enterprise Linux

HPE Cray EX235a, AMD Optimized 3rd Generation EPYC 64C 2GHz, AMD Instinct MI250X, Slingshot-11, RHEL 8.9

HPE Cray EX254n, NVIDIA Grace 72C 3.1GHz, NVIDIA GH200 Superchip, Slingshot-11, HPE Cray OS

The machine has 3.5 million node-hours (one node running for one hour) per year, half of which are reserved for Genesis Mission research. Genesis Mission was established through an executive order in November 2025 with the stated goal of creating a “dedicated, coordinated national effort to unleash a new age of AI‑accelerated innovation and discovery that can solve the most challenging problems of this century.”

More specifically, the order lays out training scientific foundation models on Federal datasets, and creating “AI agents to test new hypotheses, automate research workflows, and accelerate scientific breakthroughs.” Lux is the first dedicated supercomputer for the Genesis Mission, but it joins existing machines that have been at least partially dedicated to research, including the Intel-powered Aurora at Argonne National Laboratory, which arrived fourth in the most recent TOP500.

Lux is built primarily for AI research, not as a successor to Frontier. Discovery is on track to debut as a next-gen flagship exascale supercomputer in 2028, also developed jointly by the DOE, AMD, and HPE.

#10267. Top 6 AI Text to Speech Tools in 2026: Features, Strengths and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

This guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and plans, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

The direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt says Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Pricing: New accounts get 40 free credits. Paid plans add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

ElevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

For developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free plan includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid plans start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

Pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid plans from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

Murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

Pricing: Free plan with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

The use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

Pricing: You can start free. Paid plans are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

WellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Every voice is built from recordings of a real voice actor who consented and is paid when the voice is used, and the voices are licensed for commercial use. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

Pronunciation control is a highlight. You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

Amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for new accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example shows how little code a basic request takes:

The sample uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript, calls the neural engine and sends SSML so that the pause and emphasis are explicit. Adjust the region, voice and engine to match what your account supports.

Pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for new accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

Treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:

The say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

What is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free plans or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for new accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free plan, which has no commercial licence.

Can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid plans, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

What is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

How do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

“It’s really happening. I promise. For real.” Those are the first words from Roy Graham, head of story for Magic: The Gathering, in a video posted yesterday announcing Planeswalker, the animated series heading to Netflix in 2027.

#10265. NVIDIA brings agents to life with DGX Spark and Reachy Mini

Today at CES 2026, NVIDIA unveiled a world of new open models to enable the future of agents, online and in the real world. From the recently released NVIDIA Nemotron reasoning LLMs to the new NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1.6 open reasoning VLA and NVIDIA Cosmos world foundation models, all the building blocks are here today for AI Builders to build their own agents.

But what if you could bring your own agent to life, right at your desk? An AI buddy that can be useful to you and process your data privately?

In the CES keynote today, Jensen Huang showed us how we can do exactly that, using the processing power of NVIDIA DGX Spark with Reachy Mini to create your own little office R2D2 you can talk to and collaborate with.

This blog post provides a step-by-step guide to replicate this amazing experience at home using a DGX Spark and Reachy Mini.

If you want to start cooking right away, here’s the source code of the demo.

Feel free to adapt the recipe and make it your own - you have many ways to integrate the models into your application:

Turning an AI agent from a simple chat interface into something you can interact with naturally makes conversations feel more real. When an AI agent can see through a camera, speak out loud, and perform actions, the experience becomes more engaging. That’s what Reachy Mini makes possible.

Reachy Mini is designed to be customizable. With access to sensors, actuators, and APIs, you can easily wire it into your existing agent stack, by simulation or real hardware controlled directly from Python.

This post focuses on composing existing building blocks rather than reinventing them. We combine open models for reasoning and vision, an agent framework for orchestration, and tool handlers for actions. Each component is loosely coupled, making it easy to swap models, change routing logic, or add new behaviors.

Unlike closed personal assistants, this setup stays fully open. You control the models, the prompts, the tools, and the robot’s actions. Reachy Mini simply becomes the physical endpoint of your agent where perception, reasoning, and action come together.

In this example, we use the NVIDIA NeMo Agent Toolkit, a flexible, lightweight, framework-agnostic open source library, to connect all the components of the agent together. It works seamlessly with other agentic frameworks, like LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, handling how models interact, routing inputs and outputs between them, and making it easy to experiment with different configurations or add new capabilities without rewriting core logic. The toolkit also provides built-in profiling and optimization features, letting you track token usage efficiency and latency across tools and agents, identify bottlenecks, and automatically tune hyperparameters to maximize accuracy while reducing cost and latency.

First, clone the repository that contains all the code you’ll need to follow along:

To access your intelligence layer, powered by the NVIDIA Nemotron models, you can either deploy them using NVIDIA NIM or vLLM, or connect to them through remote endpoints available at build.nvidia.com.

The following instructions assume you are accessing the Nemotron models via endpoints. Create a .env file in the main directory with your API keys. For local deployments, you do not need to specify API keys and can skip this step.

Start by getting a basic LLM chat workflow running through NeMo Agent Toolkit’s API server. NeMo Agent Toolkit supports running workflows via `nat serve` and providing a config file. The config file passed here contains all the necessary setup information for the agent, which includes the models used for chat, image understanding, as well as the router model used by the agent. The NeMo Agent Toolkit UI can connect over HTTP/WebSocket so you can chat with your workflow like a standard chat product. In this implementation, the NeMo Agent Toolkit server is launched on port 8001 (so your bot can call it, and the UI can too):

Next, verify that you can send a plain text prompt through a separate terminal to ensure everything is setup correctly:

Reviewing the agent configuration, you’ll notice it defines far more capabilities than a simple chat completion. The next steps will walk through those details.

Tool calling is an essential part of AI agents. NeMo Agent Toolkit includes a built-in ReAct agent that can reason between tool calls and use multiple tools before answering. We route “action requests” to a ReAct agent that’s allowed to call tools (for example, tools that trigger robot behaviors or fetch current robot state).

Take a look at this portion of the config it defines the tools (like Wikipedia search) and specifies the ReAct agent pattern used to manage them.

The key idea: don’t use one model for everything. Instead, route based on intent:

You can implement routing a few ways (heuristics, a lightweight classifier, or a dedicated routing service). If you want the “production” version of this idea, the NVIDIA LLM Router developer example is the full reference implementation and includes evaluation and monitoring patterns.

A basic routing policy might work like this:

These sections of the config define the routing topology and specify the router model.

NOTE: If you want to reduce latency/cost or run offline, you can self-host one of the routed models (typically the “fast text” model) and keep the VLM remote. One common approach is serving via NVIDIA NIM or vLLM and pointing NeMo Agent Toolkit to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Now we go real time. Pipecat is a framework designed for low-latency voice/multimodal agents: it orchestrates audio/video streams, AI services, and transports so you can build natural conversations. In this repo, the bot service is responsible for:

You will find all the pipecat bot code in the `reachy-personal-assistant/bot` folder.

Reachy Mini exposes a daemon that the rest of your system connects to. The repo runs the daemon in simulation by default (--sim). If you have access to a real Reachy you can remove this flag and the same code will control your robot.

You will need three terminals to run the entire system:

If you are using the physical hardware, remember to omit the --sim flag from the command.

If the NeMo Agent Toolkit service is not already running from Step 1, start it now in Terminal 3.

Once all the terminals are set up, there are two main windows to keep track of:

Reachy Sim – This window appears automatically when you start the simulator daemon in Terminal 1. This is applicable if you’re running Reachy mini simulation in place of the physical device.

Pipecat Playground – This is the client-side UI where you can connect to the agent, enable microphone and camera inputs, and view live transcripts. In Terminal 2, open the URL exposed by the bot service: http://localhost:7860/. Click “CONNECT” in your browser. It may take a few seconds to initialize, and you’ll be prompted to grant microphone (and optionally camera) access.

At this point, you can start interacting with your agent!

Here are a few simple prompts to help you test your personal assistant. You can start with these and then experiment by adding your own to see how the agent responds!

Text-only prompts (routes to the fast text model)

Instead of a "black-box" assistant, this builds a foundation for a private, hackable system where you can control both the intelligence and the hardware. You can inspect, extend, and run it locally, with full visibility into data flow, tool permissions, and how the robot perceives and acts.

Depending on your goals, here are a few directions to explore next:

Want to try it right away? Deploy the full environment here. One click and you're running.

#10264. I’d rather use Android XR glasses over Meta Ray-Bans for the app alone

In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.

One of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration. It’s something we see frequently, and perhaps most well-known on smartwatches.

The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple. While we can’t show you the full app just yet as the one we were able to try was not completely final, it’s a very simple experience.

The app opens to an overview of your glasses to show their connection and battery status, with settings below for Gemini, apps, the camera, and more. You’ll also be able to see things such as what the various lights on the glasses mean, tutorials, and more. There’s no bloat and no messing around – it’s a utility to just make adjustments or control the glasses as needed.

You’ll probably be using this app mostly to view the photos and videos captured on Android XR glasses. Google has this set up to auto-import photos in nearly real-time. It only takes about 4 seconds to import and the process starts immediately for photos. Videos, on the other hand, take longer and may need to be manually imported (for the sake of battery in part, Google mentioned).

Across the three main platforms, there are some differences. The iPhone app doesn’t import photos quite as fast, and Samsung has its own app to fit in with One UI’s design language for Galaxy users, but the core premise is the same across all three.

While we’ll have to see how this works in real life, I was blown away by how simple it all was, though that might be because the bar is below the floor.

Meta’s Ray-Bans (and newer Meta Glasses) dominate the smart glasses conversation, and I think that the app is one of the biggest problems. It’s certainly one of the biggest reasons I’ve barely touched my Wayfarers in recent months. That’s because, in early 2025, Meta replaced its dedicated “View” app for its glasses with a Meta AI app, which is just invasive and distasteful in my book. Meta is no stranger to shoving AI down the throat of its existing users. Another well-known move was converting Facebook and Instagram search into AI search boxes with creepy levels of context and invasive actions – it makes Google’s AI Overviews look tame by comparison. But I’d argue the most aggressive was this move with its glasses. Something as simple as tweaking a setting or importing a photo now forces you to dodge an AI chatbot.

Truly, Meta’s app is the worst, and I applaud Google for building a very simple utility for Android XR glasses instead.

#10263. Researchers ‘recognize that AI will never replace HPC,’ says AMD executive — high-precision workloads will ‘exist for a very long time’ even as AI usage expands

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While AI continues to reshape industries across science and mathematics, traditional supercomputing has seemingly taken a back seat. However, AMD's Scott Tease told Tom's Hardware Premium that most HPC sites “recognize that AI will never replace HPC,” and suggests that building a heterogeneous compute stack is the best path forward to tackle bleeding-edge research, despite Nvidia pushing performance on lower-precision data types higher for AI workloads at the cost of native performance for the important double-precision FP64 format that’s critical for HPC workloads.

A heterogeneous compute stack brings together quantum, HPC, and AI under one roof, a fleet that AMD is helping pilot at Oak Ridge National Laboratory alongside IBM. Tease is AMD’s corporate vice president of HPC and sovereign AI, who joined the company earlier this year after more than a decade at Lenovo (and, before that, another 13 years at IBM). We spoke with Tease ahead of SC26 to get a read on the state of HPC, how it intersects with AI, and what’s actually driving the research community in a time when computer chips are driving headlines about international espionage plots.

FP64 is important for HPC workloads because of its precision. FP64 is a hot-button issue, largely due to how Nvidia’s GPUs have progressed over the past two generations. Or rather, how they haven't progressed. Nvidia’s latest Rubin GPU has 33 TFLOPs of FP64 compute, which is lower than the four-year-old H100’s 34 TFLOPs of FP64. For context, AMD’s year-old Instinct MI355X peaks at 78.6 TFLOPs of FP64 compute, while its upcoming HPC-angled MI430X peaks at 288 TFLOPs.

Nvidia has leaned on emulation to drive FP64 performance higher, a tactic that AMD is now pushing back on, but regardless, it’s easy to see why the HPC world could feel left behind in this new AI era. AI is defined by fuzzy, low-precision data formats, which is diametrically opposed to the accuracy of high-precision FP64. And, over the last generations of hardware from the big green giant that is Nvidia, FP64 performance has seemingly stalled in favor of driving low-precision data formats for AI workloads.

“Maybe a few years ago, people in HPC might have felt a little threatened by AI because it was taking some of the limelight,” Tease told Tom’s Hardware Premium. “But I think now they’ve come to realize that AI is an essential part of scientific discovery today. It’s just, how are you going to deploy it?”

That central question recontextualizes the apparent conflict between AI compute and HPC compute. Tease pointed to researchers spawning dozens of agents to explore viable paths for a given intent, while still leaving the complex simulations for a traditional FP64-driven HPC fleet. “...to try to do that with old approaches where you have islands of CPUs or islands of GPUs or something like that, and they're very different. They're not interconnected. It's just not going to be able to keep up,” Tease said.

One of the challenges right now is actually connecting those systems, which is an area AMD is exploring with its recent collaboration with IBM and Oak Ridge National Laboratory to deploy AMD’s “classical” computing stack in the Umbra HPC system alongside IBM’s 129-qubit Quantum Nighthawk quantum computer. The systems will connect to the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, allowing researchers to “explore how integrated quantum, AI, and scientific computing can accelerate scientific discoveries and national security.”

If the HPC crowd felt slighted by AI, you can imagine how quantum researchers probably feel.

Regardless, Tease says the future of scientific computing looks like a unified fleet that brings together AI, HPC, and quantum. “There [are] going to be a lot of problems where quantum will not be the be-all, end-all. There are some problems like human health, chemistry, where quantum’s going to allow us to do things we really can’t do with classical computing today. So having those things coexist, having them in a single workload, is where we want to get to.”

Scheduling workloads for HPC is a solved game, with open-source schedulers like Slurm driving much of the TOP500 to properly schedule workloads on supercomputers. Tease described something that goes deeper to connect these systems. “What we want to be able to do is not only do those kinds of ‘where should it go, here or there’ for HPC, we want to figure out when AI could be applied to it, when [GPU acceleration is] appropriate… and also when is it best to go in a quantum environment?”

The Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility is a test bed for figuring out how to hook these systems together properly. The press release explicitly states that it’s a “shared environment to evaluate the architectures, software, and workflows that future hybrid quantum systems will require.” The system is a co-design initiative with IBM, bringing together quantum and classical computing into one system.

With the system, researchers are exploring how to accelerate quantum error correction with classical systems, a critical step in quantum computing to weed out environmental influences. The goal is ultimately to accelerate quantum systems in the Quantum Genesis Q competition, an initiative launched by the U.S. Department of Energy that will provide up to $215 million in funding for quantum research.

By late 2028, the competition calls for quantum computers “with at least 100 logical qubits that are capable of performing hundreds of millions [of] fault-tolerant operations.” IBM describes the error correction research that will be performed at Oak Ridge as a “key component” in driving toward that goal. Separately, AMD announced last week an investment in quantum outfit PsiQuantum to provide CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs to drive the company’s first fault-tolerant quantum system.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

#10262. This Quest 3 golf club actually improved my scores, but it comes at a cost

The AMVR GA2 is a fresh take on a Quest 3 golf club accessory, and I was pleasantly surprised with what it did for my scores.

In the past decade of covering VR devices and accessories, I’ve used a lot of golf clubs. Short clubs. Long clubs. Adjustable length clubs. Clubs with realistic weight. Even a club with a magnet inside that makes a convincing “thwack!” sound every time you swing it. But the AMVR GA2’s inclusion of a proper club head at the bottom does something fascinating for its physics, and I immediately noticed the difference at the end of the first course I played with this Quest 3 golf club.

Most VR golf club accessories, including the first-gen AMVR GA1, stick the controller at the bottom of the shaft where the head usually goes. This makes sense since you don’t hit a real ball with a VR golf club accessory; it’s all virtual. But, ironically, putting a proper golf club head on the end (and the controller in the middle of the shaft) apparently does make a difference. This one works with both the Meta Quest 3 and Quest 3S, but not the older Meta Quest 2 or Quest Pro.

I’m not going to delve into the physics of why this works, but it’s likely that shifting the fulcrum point improves it. I didn’t expect this at all. When AMVR told me about their new club, I accepted because the company typically makes top-notch accessories. I really didn’t need another club in my extensive Quest 3 golf club collection. But I’m glad I did, because I’ve done much better than usual in my weekly Walkabout Mini Golf rounds with friends since I got it.

The mechanism for securing the controller onto the club is identical to previous AMVR controllers; only the location of the mount is different. Slide the controller (with wrist strap attached) into the holster. Click the rubber stopper in so the controller doesn’t move, then loop the wrist strap around the controller as a backup in case you didn’t secure the rubber stopper properly. It’s quite simple.

All major VR golf games allow custom spacing for Quest 3 golf clubs, so it doesn’t take more than 30 seconds to get comfortable with the club in your game of choice.

The only problem I’ve found with this club is its price. Most Quest 3 golf club accessories cost between $30 and $50, depending on the capabilities. This one is normally double that, but AMVR was kind enough to pass along a 25% off coupon for 9to5Google readers, making it more palatable if you’re looking to improve your VR golf scores. Just apply the coupon code 1FD4JYT5 at checkout on Amazon for an extra 25% off the AMVR GA2 golf club.

If you’re serious about your scores in Golf+, Walkabout Mini Golf, or another favorite of yours, this might just be the ultimate enthusiast Quest 3 golf club accessory.
